The props are `OverlayProps`; declare only the ones you read. Pass the component to whatever
is dragged:

```ts
import TicketOverlay from './TicketOverlay.vue';

makeSortableList(listRef, { items: tickets, overlay: TicketOverlay });   // every item of the list
makeSortableItem(el, { item: () => props.ticket, overlay: TicketOverlay }); // this item
makeDraggable(el, { id: 'chip', overlay: TicketOverlay });                // a plain draggable
```

A component can be passed as it is, in a `shallowRef` to switch it (mid-drag too: the overlay
changes at once), or as a function, which Vue takes as a functional component:
`overlay: (props) => <TicketOverlay {...props} compact />` in TSX. Never put it in a deep
`ref` or `reactive`: Vue would make the component reactive and warn.

The root of an overlay component should fill the box (`width: 100%; height: 100%`): the box
takes the size of the slot and animates it on drop. A fixed size on the root keeps that size
inside the box instead.

## The provider's `#overlay` slot

For every drag without a component of its own, the provider's slot renders the overlay.
Define it once, next to your app's root, and every list and draggable in the app gets it.
Here notes get a ghost of their own, and photos fall back to the clone:

<example height="26rem" hint="Drag a note, then a photo" name="overlay-slot">



</example>

```vue [App.vue]
<DnDProvider>
  <RouterView />
  <template #overlay="{ items, status }">
    <NoteGhost v-if="items[0]?.type.includes('note')" :items="items" :status="status" />
  </template>
</DnDProvider>
```

The slot gets the same props as an overlay component. When it renders nothing (the
`v-if` above), the drag falls back to the clone. Tell drags apart by `type`: a sortable
item's type is its group's name unless it sets its own (`makeSortableItem(el, { type })`).

## Targets that change the overlay

A drop target can say what the overlay shows while a drag it takes is over it.
`makeDroppable`, lists and trees take an `overOverlay` (a list's or tree's `overlay` is
for its own items). Over a folder, the chip of the dragged messages turns into
what the drop will do:

<example height="34rem" hint="Tick two messages, drag one over Archive and let go" name="overlay-folders">



</example>

```ts [Folder.vue]
makeDroppable(el, {
  id: () => props.folder.id,
  data: () => props.folder,
  overOverlay: MovePill,
  onDrop: (event) => emit('move', event.active.ids),
});
```

The target's component gets the same props as any overlay component, `over` among them,
and the drag's own overlay (its component, the provider's slot or the clone) as its default
slot. `MovePill` leaves the slot out, so it replaces the chip:

```vue [MovePill.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
import { computed } from 'vue';
import type { DragItem, Over } from '@vue-dnd-kit/core';

const props = defineProps<{ items: DragItem[]; over: Over | null }>();
// The folder under the drag: its `data`.
const folder = computed(() => props.over?.data as Folder | undefined);
</script>

<template>
  <!-- Fills the box like any overlay component. -->
  <div class="pill-box">
    <span v-if="folder" class="pill">Move {{ items.length }} to {{ folder.name }}</span>
  </div>
</template>
```

Render `<slot />` to keep the drag's own overlay and wrap it. That is what Done does in the
board of [overlay components](#overlay-components) above: over Done, an approved ticket
keeps its own overlay, Done stamps it, and a ticket from another column gets confetti when
it is dropped.

```ts [Column.vue]
makeSortableList(listRef, {
  items: tickets,
  group: { name: 'release', put },
  overlay: TicketOverlay, // the tickets' own, in every column
  overOverlay: strict ? DoneOverlay : undefined, // Done's, around it
});
```

```vue [DoneOverlay.vue]
<template>
  <div class="done">
    <slot /> <!-- TicketOverlay -->
    <span class="stamp">Shipped</span>
    <span v-if="status === 'dropping' && arrives" class="confetti">…</span>
  </div>
</template>
```

- It shows only while the target accepts the drag, and stays while the drop lands on it.
Leaving the target brings the drag's own overlay back.
- The change crossfades. The provider's `overlayTransition` sets how: `false` swaps at once,
an object is the props of a `<Transition>` around the content (`name`, `mode`, JS hooks
for GSAP or motion). Without `mode: 'out-in'` both show for a moment: give the leaving one
`position: absolute` in `.<name>-leave-active`.
- The drop waits for the confetti: CSS animations and transitions that run in the overlay
as it lands play to their end, for two seconds at most.
- A drag with `overlay: false` has no overlay over any target.

The folders also land the pill their own way, into the folder's icon: a target can have an
`overDropAnimation` too. See [animations](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/animations#per-item-and-per-target).

## Where the drop would go: `to`

`to` tells an overlay where a drop would put the items now, as the drop event's `to` will:
the list and the index there, and in a tree the parent and the depth. It changes as the slot
moves. A page of this site menu says which section it would go into, and at which row:

<example height="27rem" hint="Drag a page over the sections, then sideways to change its depth" name="overlay-move-path">



</example>

```vue [MoveOverlay.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
import { computed } from 'vue';
import type { DragItem, DropDestination } from '@vue-dnd-kit/core';

const props = defineProps<{ items: DragItem[]; to: DropDestination | null }>();
const page = computed(() => props.items[0]!.item as MenuNode);
// `parentKey` is the section the page would go into, `null` at the top level.
const where = computed(() => (props.to ? pathOf(menu.value, props.to.parentKey) : null));
</script>

<template>
  <div class="move">
    <div class="row">{{ page.title }}</div>
    <p v-if="to && where" class="where">Move to <b>{{ where }}</b>, row {{ to.index + 1 }}</p>
  </div>
</template>
```

Outside every target, `to` is still the slot's place: by default a drop there keeps the items
where the slot is (`dropOutside: 'placeholder'`). It is `null` when the drop would put them in
no list: over a plain target, over a list that refuses them, outside with
`dropOutside: 'cancel'` or `'remove'`.

## What wins

For each drag, the first one that applies:

1. The drop target's `overOverlay` (a list's or tree's too), while the drag is over it
and it accepts the drag. What would show otherwise is its default slot.
2. The item's own `overlay` (`makeSortableItem`, `makeDraggable`).
3. Its list's or tree's `overlay`.
4. The provider's `#overlay` slot, unless it renders nothing.
5. The default clone. In a multi-drag, a column or a pile of clones: see
[multi-drag](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/multi-drag#the-default-overlay).

Whether a drag has an overlay at all (`overlay: false`) is decided when it starts. Which
component shows is read live: a ref switched mid-drag swaps it, and so does entering or
leaving a target with an overlay of its own.

## `DragPreview`: the clone in your layout

`DragPreview` renders the library's clone of one dragged item. An overlay component can
lay out several of them, or put a frame around one. Click books to pick them, then drag
one: the overlay fans out the real clones.

<example height="24rem" hint="Drag one of the three picked books; click books to pick others" name="overlay-fan">



</example>

```vue [FanOverlay.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
import { computed } from 'vue';
import { DragPreview, type DragItem } from '@vue-dnd-kit/core';

const props = defineProps<{ items: DragItem[] }>();
const fan = computed(() =>
  props.items.slice(0, 4).map((entry, index) => ({
    entry,
    angle: index === 0 ? 0 : (index % 2 ? -1 : 1) * Math.ceil(index / 2) * 10,
  })),
);
</script>

<template>
  <div class="fan">
    <div v-for="{ entry, angle } in fan" :key="entry.id" class="card" :style="{ transform: `rotate(${angle}deg)` }">
      <DragPreview :id="entry.id" class="face" :style="{ width: '100%', height: '100%' }">
        <div class="blank" /> <!-- an item without a clone -->
      </DragPreview>
    </div>
    <span v-if="items.length > 1" class="count">{{ items.length }}</span>
  </div>
</template>
```

- Clones exist for the grabbed item and the others next to it in drop order, as many as the
provider's `overlayPreviews` (5 by default, `'all'` for every one), if they are rendered at
pickup. For any other item, `DragPreview` renders its default slot.
- A preview has its item's size at pickup, set inline. Size it with `style`, which falls
through (a class can't override it), as above.
- In a sortable multi-drag (`multiple: 'group'` or `'gaps'`), each preview lands on its own
item's slot on drop. Turn its wrappers with `transform` (not the `rotate` property): the
landing undoes it on the way. Put the item's look (corners, shadow) on the preview
itself, as `class="face"` does: the wrappers stay in the box.

The [multi-drag guide](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/multi-drag#a-custom-overlay-for-several-items) has an
overlay that shows a count and the titles instead of the clones.

## Size: `overlayFit`

Over a list of other sizes, the box takes the size of the slot it will land in. The provider's
`overlayFit` switches it; the [DnDProvider page](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/api/dnd-provider) has a demo with a
narrow and a wide list.

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      <code>
        overlayFit
      </code>
      
       (provider)
    </th>
    
    <th>
      The box
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        'slot'
      </code>
      
       (default)
    </td>
    
    <td>
      Takes the size of the slot it will land in, gliding to it. Over the wide list, it widens.
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        'source'
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      Keeps the dragged element's size.
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

With `'slot'`, the box resizes around the pointer, which stays at the same fraction of the
box. The content is never scaled: it re-lays out at the new size, so a flex row like the
tasks of that demo looks right at any width. A slot styled much smaller than the item, such as a
thin line, doesn't shrink the box along that axis.

A drop does the same with either setting: the box flies to the landing element and
animates to **its** size, and the content re-lays out on the way. When an item looks
different in two lists (a compact chip in a palette, a full card on a board), the clone of
the source re-lays out at the target's size, and may look squeezed or stretched there. Two
ways to keep it right:

- Give the item a **layout that works at both sizes**, as the task rows do, or the same
size in every list it can land in.
- Render the **target's look** in an overlay component. It gets `over`, so it can switch
to the look of the list it is over, and it fills the box at any size.

## Where it renders: `overlayTo`

The provider teleports the overlay to `body`. A modal `<dialog>` (opened with
`showModal()`) sits on the top layer, above everything in `body`, so an overlay there would
be hidden under it. Point `overlayTo` at a selector or an element inside the dialog. The
[DnDProvider page](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/api/dnd-provider#where-the-overlay-renders) has a dialog to try it
with and without:

```vue [index.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
const dialog = useTemplateRef<HTMLDialogElement>('dialog');
const open = ref(false);
// While the dialog is open, the overlay renders inside it.
const overlayTo = computed(() => (open.value ? '#columns-dialog' : 'body'));

const show = () => {
  dialog.value?.showModal();
  open.value = true;
};
</script>

<template>
  <DnDProvider :overlay-to="overlayTo">
    <button type="button" @click="show">Edit columns</button>
    <dialog id="columns-dialog" ref="dialog" @close="open = false">
      <ColumnList v-model:columns="columns" />
    </dialog>
  </DnDProvider>
</template>
```

- The target must be in the page when the provider renders the overlay, after it mounts. A
closed `<dialog>` is: it is only hidden. Switch back to `body` while it is closed, so the
overlay of other drags shows.
- The box is `position: fixed`. A `transform`, `filter` or `contain` on the target or its
ancestors makes it the box's frame instead of the viewport, so keep them off the dialog.
- The clone's styles are computed for where it is shown: in a shadow root, point
`overlayTo` inside it and the clone keeps the shadow root's styles.

## No overlay

`makeDraggable(el, { overlay: false })` has no box at all: the element itself moves,
through the returned `transform`.

```ts
const { transform } = makeDraggable(el, { overlay: false });
const style = computed(() =>
  transform.value ? { translate: `${transform.value.x}px ${transform.value.y}px` } : undefined,
);
```

See [drag and drop](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/drag-and-drop#without-an-overlay). How a drag with a box
lands is its `dropAnimation`: the drop target's (`overDropAnimation`), the item's (or its list's), or the
provider's. See
[animations](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/animations#the-drop).

- **Page:** Multi-drag and selection
- **Source:** https://zizigy.github.io/vue-dnd-kit/docs/guides/multi-drag
- **Description:** Select several items with clicks or a rubber band and drag them together — as a block, leaving gaps, or stacked into the overlay — take only some of them on drop, and show them in an overlay of your own.

Select a few files, then drag one of them: the others come along. Switch `multiple` to see

## The selection

Each provider keeps one selection: a reactive set of ids. Dragging a **selected** item
drags every selected item, the grabbed one first. Dragging an item that isn't selected
drags only that item.

The library doesn't decide how people select: the click rules are yours. It never clears
the selection on its own either, and the selection survives unmounts, such as the rows a
virtual list recycles.

### Clicks: Ctrl/Cmd and Shift

Every sortable item and draggable returns `selected`, a writable ref bound to the
selection. Bind it to a class, a checkbox (`v-model="selected"`), or set it in a click
handler:

```vue [FileItem.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
const { selected } = makeSortableItem(el, { item: () => props.file });
</script>

<template>
  <li ref="el" class="file" :class="{ selected }" @click="emit('pick', $event)">…</li>
</template>
```

The demo's list owns the rules: a click selects one file, Ctrl/Cmd-click adds or removes
one, Shift-click selects the run from the last clicked file:

```ts [Files.vue]
const { selection } = useDnD();
let anchor: string | null = null;

const pick = (id: string, event: MouseEvent) => {
  const ids = items.value.map((file) => file.id);
  if (event.shiftKey && anchor) {
    const [a, b] = [ids.indexOf(anchor), ids.indexOf(id)];
    selection.set(ids.slice(Math.min(a, b), Math.max(a, b) + 1));
    return;
  }
  if (event.ctrlKey || event.metaKey) selection.toggle(id);
  else selection.set([id]);
  anchor = id;
};
```

The click that ends a drag doesn't reach `@click`, so a drop never changes the selection
by accident. Use `@click`, not `pointerup`, for item actions.

### From anywhere: `useDnD().selection`

```ts
import { useDnD, useDnDMonitor } from '@vue-dnd-kit/core';

const { selection } = useDnD();

selection.has('a');               // is it selected?
selection.add('a', 'b');          // select
selection.delete('a');            // deselect
selection.toggle('a');            // flip it, or force it: toggle('a', true)
selection.set(['a', 'c']);        // exactly these
selection.clear();
selection.ids;                    // a reactive ReadonlySet<Key>

// Clear it after every drop, if your UI wants that:
useDnDMonitor({ onDragEnd: () => selection.clear() });
```

The selection is keyed by id, so it can hold items of several lists, and plain draggables
too: a drag takes every selected item under the provider.

## Rubber-band selection

`makeSelectionArea` turns an element into an area where a press on the empty space draws
a band, and the items it crosses are selected. On this desktop, draw a band around a few
icons, then drag one of them:

<example height="29rem" hint="Draw a box on the empty desktop, then drag a selected icon" name="multi-select">



</example>

```vue [Desktop.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
const desktop = useTemplateRef<HTMLElement>('desktop');
const { isSelecting, style } = makeSelectionArea(desktop);
</script>

<template>
  <!-- The area needs a position: the band is placed inside it. -->
  <div ref="desktop" class="desktop">
    <DesktopIcon v-for="icon in icons" :key="icon.id" :icon="icon" />
    <div v-if="isSelecting" class="band" :style="style" />
  </div>
</template>

<style scoped>
.desktop { position: relative; height: 236px; }
.band { border: 1px solid #42b883; background: color-mix(in srgb, #42b883 15%, transparent); }
</style>
```

- You render the band: `style` places it, relative to the area's content.
- The area needs a **non-static position** (`relative` will do), or the band lands
somewhere else.
- A band starts only from the area itself, so make the area large: the whole panel, with
space around the items, not a tight wrapper.
- A press on an item drags it. Buttons, fields and the area's scrollbar keep their
presses.
- The band stays anchored to the content while the area or the page scrolls.
<kbd value="Escape">



</kbd>

 cancels it and restores the selection.
- `useDnD().status` is `'selecting'` while a band is drawn: the line under the desktop
reads it.

`strategy`, `modifier` and `disabled` take a value, a ref or a getter, read when a press
starts a band. With areas inside areas, the innermost one takes the press. The
[makeSelectionArea API](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/api/make-selection-area) page switches them live.

### Moving them as they lie

The icons are plain draggables (`makeDraggable`), each with its icon as `data`. Their
overlay is a component of the demo's own: it lays a `DragPreview` of every dragged icon out
as the icons lie on the desktop, around the grabbed one. The icons wait in place, dimmed by
`isDragging`, which stays `true` until their copies have landed.

```vue [Formation.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
const props = defineProps<{ items: DragItem[] }>();

const placed = computed(() => {
  const grabbed = props.items[0]!.data as Icon;
  return props.items.map(({ id, data }) => {
    const icon = data as Icon;
    return { id, left: `${icon.x - grabbed.x}px`, top: `${icon.y - grabbed.y}px` };
  });
});
</script>

<template>
  <div class="formation">
    <DragPreview v-for="{ id, left, top } in placed" :id="id" :key="id" class="copy" :style="{ left, top }" />
  </div>
</template>
```

```ts [DesktopIcon.vue]
const { isDragging, selected } = makeDraggable(el, { id, data: () => props.icon, overlay: Formation });
```

The desktop takes the drop. Its `position` is where the grabbed icon was let go, in the
desktop's coordinates: the icon goes there, and the others move as far. Each copy then lands
on its own icon in its new place. Dropped off the desktop, the copies fly back to the icons.

```ts [Desktop.vue]
makeDroppable(desktop, {
  id: 'desktop',
  onDrop: ({ active, position }) => {
    const grabbed = icons.value.find((icon) => icon.id === active.id)!;
    const shift = { x: position!.x - grabbed.x, y: position!.y - grabbed.y };
    for (const icon of icons.value) {
      if (!active.ids.includes(icon.id)) continue;
      icon.x += shift.x; // the demo also keeps each icon on the desktop
      icon.y += shift.y;
    }
  },
});
```

A clone is taken at pickup for at most 5 items by default: the provider's
`overlay-previews="all"` takes one for every selected icon.

### Into a folder

In this window the band selects files, and folders take them. The overlay is the default
one: a pile of the picked files. Dropped into a folder, they go in one after another, the
grabbed one last, and the folder gulps. Cancelled, each flies back to its file. Click a
folder to open it, and drag files back to Home in the path.

<example height="33rem" hint="Draw a box around a few files, drag them onto a folder" name="multi-finder">



</example>

```vue [index.vue]
<!-- Every picked file gets a clone at pickup: they all go in. -->
<DnDProvider overlay-previews="all">
  <Finder />
</DnDProvider>
```

```ts [FolderTile.vue]
makeDroppable(el, {
  id: () => props.folder.id,
  accept: 'file',
  onDrop: (event) => emit('move', event.active.ids),
});

// The files are in: the folder gulps.
useDnDMonitor({
  onDragSettle: (event) => {
    if ('dropped' in event && event.over?.id === props.folder.id) gulps.value++;
  },
});
```

That is all it takes: the files leave the window with the drop, so they have nowhere to land
but the folder, and the default drop animation sends a multi-drag into a zone one item after
another. `overlayPreviews` says how many items get a clone at pickup (5 by default). Every
clone flies: into the zone, to its slot, or back to its item.

The folder is a button: a band never starts on buttons and fields, so a click opens it.

## How the other items move: `multiple`

The list where a multi-drag starts decides what the other selected items do while it
runs. Switch it in the first demo on this page:

```ts
makeSortableList(listRef, { items: files, multiple: 'gaps' });
```

On drop, the items land together at the target index, in the order they had. In
`'group'` and `'gaps'`, each item of the overlay flies to its own slot. The option is read
when a drag starts, so a ref or a getter switches it.

Over a drop target that is no list, such as a trash can or a playlist, or over a list that
refuses the drag, a `'group'` block comes apart: every item shows in its own place again,
as a drop there leaves it, and the block forms again once a list is hovered.

Style the items left behind in `'gaps'`, faded by default:

```css
.file[data-dnd-dragging] {
  opacity: 0.35;
}
```

### The default overlay

In `'group'` and `'gaps'`, the overlay is a column of the dragged items as they will land:
the grabbed one under the pointer, the others before and after it in drop order (a row in
horizontal lists). It shows as many as the provider's `overlayPreviews` (5 by default,
`'all'` for every rendered one). The ones past that are counted where they are: `+N` at the
start of the column for the items that land before the shown ones, `+N` at the end for
those after.

In grids, a column of whole cells would cover the page, so the overlay is a pile: up to
three items fanned out behind the grabbed one, with the total count on top. Switch the demo
to Grid to see it.

Plain draggables (`makeDraggable`) make a pile too, as the files above do. Every clone in
the overlay lands on its own: on its slot after a drop into a list, on its item wherever the
drop left it (back in place after a cancel), and into the zone a drop goes into when the
items are gone from the page, one after another, the box last.

## Taking only some

A list's `onBeforeDrop` can accept part of a multi-drag: return the keys it takes, and the
others fly back where they came from. It may be async, and ask: the overlay waits where it
was let go until the answer comes. Here Scheduled wants posts with a cover. Dropped with one
that has none, it asks whether to add the missing covers and take them all, take only the
ready posts, or none:

<example height="28.5rem" hint="Drag the three picked drafts into Scheduled, then answer" name="multi-transfer">



</example>

```ts [PostList.vue]
const { items } = makeSortableList(list, {
  id: props.id,
  items: posts,
  group: 'blog',
  onBeforeDrop: async (event) => {
    const missing = event.items.filter((post) => post.cover === null);
    if (!props.ask || event.sameList || !missing.length) return true;
    const choice = await props.ask(missing, event.items.length - missing.length); // the question under the lists
    if (choice === 'cover') missing.forEach((post) => (post.cover = pickCover()));
    if (choice === 'ready') return event.keys.filter((_, index) => event.items[index]!.cover !== null);
    return choice === 'cover'; // all of them, or none: they fly back
  },
});
```

- `event.keys` are the dragged keys, and `event.items[i]` is the item of `event.keys[i]`.
- After the answer, `onDrop` gets `accepted` and `rejected`, and `event.result` holds the
lists as the partial drop leaves them.
- While the drop waits, the lists keep showing every dragged post where it would land: the
answer decides. For a rule that needs no question, `group.put` decides while hovering
(see [mixed types](#mixed-types) below). More in
[drop decisions](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/drop-decisions).

### A limit

On this board, In progress and Review have a limit of cards. A full column takes nothing:
its `group.put` refuses, and the pile turns red over it. A column with room for some of
the picked cards takes as many as fit, and the others fly back. The column's overlay says
so before the drop.

<example height="31rem" hint="Tick three cards in To do, drag one over Review, then In progress" name="multi-wip">



</example>

```ts [WipColumn.vue]
const room = (keys: Key[]) => limit - column.cards.filter((card) => !keys.includes(card.id)).length;

makeSortableList(list, {
  items: cards,
  group: { name: 'board', put: ({ keys, from, to }) => from === to || room(keys) > 0 },
  multiple: 'stack',
  overlay: CardPile, // red where `accepted` is false
  overOverlay: fit,
  onBeforeDrop: (event) => {
    if (event.sameList) return true;
    const free = room(event.keys);
    return free >= event.keys.length || event.keys.slice(0, free);
  },
});
```

`fit` is a function, which Vue takes as a functional component. It gives `FitBadge` what
only the column knows, its room, and passes the pile on as the badge's slot.

```ts
const fit: FunctionalComponent<OverlayProps> = (overlay, { slots }) =>
  h(FitBadge, { count: overlay.items.length, room: room(overlay.items.map((item) => item.id)), limit }, slots);
```

### Mixed types

A list can also refuse some items by their type, before the drop. With `acceptMode: 'some'`,
`group.put` is asked for each item on its own: the list takes the drag when at least one
item fits, and the rest fly back on drop. With `'all'` (the default), every item must fit.

```ts
makeSortableList(gallery, {
  items: photos,
  group: { name: 'files', put: ({ types }) => types.includes('image') },
  acceptMode: 'some',
});
```

Plain drop targets take `acceptMode` too. See
[lists that share items](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/shared-lists#limits) and
[drag and drop](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/drag-and-drop#which-drags-a-target-takes).

## A custom overlay for several items

Overlay components and the provider's `#overlay` slot get `items`: every dragged item, the
grabbed one first. Show a summary instead of the items themselves: here a count, the first
subject, and what the drop will do.

<example height="26rem" hint="Drag the checked mails to Archive or Trash, or drag one alone" name="multi-summary">



</example>

```vue [MailOverlay.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
import { computed } from 'vue';
import type { DragItem, Over } from '@vue-dnd-kit/core';

const props = defineProps<{ items: DragItem[]; over: Over | null }>();

const first = computed(() => props.items[0]?.item as Mail);
const count = computed(() => props.items.length);
// What the drop does, from the `data` of the zone under it.
const zone = computed(() => props.over?.data as { verb: string; danger?: boolean } | undefined);
const action = computed(() => {
  const noun = count.value === 1 ? 'conversation' : 'conversations';
  return `${zone.value?.verb ?? 'Move'} ${count.value} ${noun}`;
});
</script>

<template>
  <!-- The box keeps the row's size; the summary hangs off its middle, by the pointer. -->
  <div class="box">
    <div class="summary" :class="{ stack: count > 1, danger: zone?.danger }">
      <span class="count">{{ count }}</span>
      <strong>{{ action }}</strong>
      <small>{{ first.subject }}{{ count > 1 ? ` and ${count - 1} more` : '' }}</small>
    </div>
  </div>
</template>

<style scoped>
.box { position: relative; width: 100%; height: 100%; }
.summary { position: absolute; top: calc(50% + 10px); left: calc(50% + 10px); width: 230px; }
</style>
```

```ts [Mailbox.vue]
// The box is centered on the pointer, so the summary hangs off the pointer and leaves
// the zone under it in sight.
const { items } = makeSortableList(list, { items: mails, overlay: MailOverlay, modifiers: [snapCenterToCursor] });

// A zone takes the mails out of the inbox; its `data` tells the overlay what it does.
makeDroppable(archive, {
  id: 'Archive',
  data: { verb: 'Archive' },
  onDrop: (event) => {
    event.source?.remove();
    selection.clear();
  },
});
```

To lay out the real items instead, render their clones with `DragPreview`, as the
[desktop](#moving-them-as-they-lie) above does; the
[overlay guide](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/overlay#dragpreview-the-clone-in-your-layout) fans out a stack
of books. Clones are taken at pickup for the grabbed item and the others next to it in drop
order, as many as `overlayPreviews`; for any other item, `DragPreview` renders its default
slot. Each preview lands on its own item on drop.

## Trees

In a tree, the selected nodes move as one block, each with its subtree, in document order.
A selected node inside another selected one rides along in its parent's subtree. See
[trees](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/trees).

---

- **Page:** Virtual lists
- **Source:** https://zizigy.github.io/vue-dnd-kit/docs/guides/virtual-lists
- **Description:** Sort thousands of rows with TanStack Virtual or VueUse's useVirtualList — feed the virtualizer the draft, key rows by id, and keep the dragged row mounted.

Sorting is data-driven: the draft `items` is a new array on every reorder, rows are keyed by item,
and the animations only need the rows that are mounted. So any virtualizer that renders from an
array works — feed it the draft instead of your array.

<example height="32.5rem" hint="10,000 rows, a handful in the DOM: drag one, or scroll while you drag" name="virtual-list">



</example>

## The rules

1. Give the virtualizer the **draft items**, not your source array.
2. **Key rows by the item's key**, never by index. The official TanStack and VueUse examples key by
index; change that.
3. Pass ids to `makeSortableItem` as a **getter**, `{ id: () => props.item.id }`: the virtualizer
may hand a row component another item.
4. Hold big arrays in a **shallowRef**. The library never deep-traverses your data.
5. Keep the placeholder the same size as the row: hide its content, don't collapse it.
6. Overscan at least 5 rows (VueUse: at least 1), so rows are mounted before auto-scroll reaches
them.
7. Don't animate rows' `height`, `margin` or `padding`, and don't put `will-change` on the
scroller.

## VueUse useVirtualList

The demo above. Every row has the same height, and VueUse's math stays O(1):

```vue [TaskList.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
import { shallowRef, useTemplateRef } from 'vue';
import { useVirtualList } from '@vueuse/core';
import { makeSortableList } from '@vue-dnd-kit/core';

const ROW = 44;
const tasks = shallowRef(makeTasks(10_000));

// The outer element is the sortable list: `containerProps` owns the scroller's ref.
const listRef = useTemplateRef<HTMLElement>('list');
const { items } = makeSortableList(listRef, { items: tasks });

// Fed with the draft `items`, so the rows move while you drag.
const { list, containerProps, wrapperProps } = useVirtualList(items, { itemHeight: ROW, overscan: 8 });
</script>

<template>
  <div ref="list">
    <div v-bind="containerProps" style="height: 308px">
      <div v-bind="wrapperProps">
        <!-- Keyed by id, not by index as in VueUse's docs. -->
        <Row v-for="{ data } in list" :key="data.id" :task="data" :height="ROW" />
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</template>
```

- `itemHeight` is the row's real height, borders included. Put no margins between rows: VueUse
doesn't count them.
- The sortable list is the outer element, because `containerProps` binds its own `ref` to the
scroller. Auto-scroll still finds the scroller: it scrolls the containers under the pointer.
- VueUse can't keep a row mounted: the dragged row unmounts when you scroll it away. That's fine,
see [What stays mounted](#what-stays-mounted).

## TanStack Virtual

TanStack measures every row, so rows can be as tall as their content. It can also keep the dragged
row mounted however far you scroll from it:

<example height="34.5rem" hint="Drag a note just below the list and hold: the dragged row stays pinned" name="virtual-tanstack">



</example>

```vue [NoteList.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
import { computed, shallowRef, useTemplateRef } from 'vue';
import { defaultRangeExtractor, useVirtualizer, type Range } from '@tanstack/vue-virtual';
import { makeSortableList } from '@vue-dnd-kit/core';

const notes = shallowRef(makeNotes(5_000));

// The scroller is the sortable list: the library sorts it and auto-scrolls it.
const scrollRef = useTemplateRef<HTMLElement>('scroll');
const { items, activeIndex, captureLayout } = makeSortableList(scrollRef, { items: notes });

// One computed that reads the draft once: TanStack memoizes the measurements and the range
// on `getItemKey` and `rangeExtractor`, so they must be new functions after every reorder.
const virtualizer = useVirtualizer(
  computed(() => {
    const arr = items.value;
    const pin = activeIndex.value;
    return {
      count: arr.length,
      getScrollElement: () => scrollRef.value,
      estimateSize: () => 92,
      overscan: 6,
      getItemKey: (index: number) => arr[index]!.id,
      // The dragged row stays mounted, however far you scroll from it.
      rangeExtractor: (range: Range) => {
        const indexes = defaultRangeExtractor(range);
        return pin < 0 || indexes.includes(pin) ? indexes : [...indexes, pin].sort((a, b) => a - b);
      },
      // Measurements land after the library's animation pass: animate them too.
      onChange: () => captureLayout(),
    };
  }),
);
const rows = computed(() => virtualizer.value.getVirtualItems());
const measure = (el: unknown) => virtualizer.value.measureElement(el as HTMLElement | null);
</script>

<template>
  <div ref="scroll" style="height: 340px; overflow: auto; contain: strict">
    <div :style="{ height: `${virtualizer.getTotalSize()}px`, position: 'relative' }">
      <div
        v-for="row in rows"
        :key="(row.key as string)"
        :ref="measure"
        :data-index="row.index"
        :style="{ position: 'absolute', top: 0, left: 0, width: '100%', transform: `translateY(${row.start}px)` }"
      >
        <NoteRow :note="items[row.index]!" />
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</template>
```

What each piece does:

When does the dragged row leave the range? Its slot follows the pointer while the pointer is over
the list. Move the pointer just below the list and hold it there: auto-scroll goes on, the slot
stays where it was, and soon it is far above the rows on screen. The pin keeps it mounted, so the
drop lands on a real element. A list with `placeholder: 'indicator'` keeps the dragged row in place
for the whole drag, so there it matters even more.

- Pinning needs rows positioned one by one, absolutely, as above. A virtualizer that renders one
padded block can't add a row far away.
- The row component passes its id as a getter: `makeSortableItem(el, { id: () => props.note.id })`.
- Keep TanStack's `anchorTo: 'start'`, the default. With `lanes`, use `@tanstack/virtual-core` 3.19
or newer (`@tanstack/vue-virtual` installs it).

## Virtual kanban columns

Each column is its own sortable list and its own virtualizer, and the lists share a `group`. Three
columns of 1,000 cards render a few dozen:

<example height="34rem" hint="Move a card between columns of 1,000 cards" name="virtual-kanban">



</example>

A card coming in from another column has no measurement in this column yet. Estimate it at the
dragged card's real size, `activeSize`, read in the same computed:

```ts [Column.vue]
const { items, activeIndex, activeSize, captureLayout } = makeSortableList(scrollRef, {
  id: props.column.id,
  items: props.column.cards, // a shallowRef per column
  group: 'board',
});

const virtualizer = useVirtualizer(
  computed(() => {
    const arr = items.value;
    const pin = activeIndex.value;
    const size = activeSize.value;
    return {
      count: arr.length,
      getScrollElement: () => scrollRef.value,
      // A card coming from another column gets its real height before it is measured.
      estimateSize: (index: number) => (index === pin && size ? size.height + GAP : 72),
      // …getItemKey, rangeExtractor and onChange as above
    };
  }),
);
```

- Give each column its data as a `shallowRef`: the list writes its drops into it, and 1,000 cards
get no deep proxies.
- `activeSize` is the size of the dragged element at the start of the drag. Add what your slot puts
around the card: here the gap under it (`GAP`) is the slot's padding, so the virtualizer measures
it too.
- The header counts `items.length`, the draft: it changes the moment a card enters or leaves.

## What stays mounted

The dragged row may unmount while you drag: it scrolled out of range, or the virtualizer recycled
its component. The drag survives it. The overlay keeps showing the item, the selection is kept by
id, and the item lands where the draft puts it. Animations only touch the rows that are mounted.

Where the virtualizer can, keep the dragged row mounted anyway, as the TanStack recipe does with
`rangeExtractor`. The list tells you which row that is:

## Trees

`makeSortableTree` returns a flat `items` of the visible rows, so a tree virtualizes like a list:
keyed by `node.key`, with `activeIndex` and `activeKey` naming the row to keep mounted. See
[Trees](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/trees).

---

- **Page:** Introduction
- **Source:** https://zizigy.github.io/vue-dnd-kit/docs/getting-started/introduction
- **Description:** Vue DnD Kit is drag and drop for Vue 3 — sortable lists, kanban boards, trees, multi-drag and drop zones, animated and accessible out of the box.

Vue DnD Kit is drag and drop for Vue 3. Sortable lists, kanban boards, trees, multi-drag, copying
and drop zones — animated, keyboard-ready and announced to screen readers out of the box, in your
own markup.

<example height="27rem" hint="Move stops between days; the chips below name the other gestures" name="at-a-glance" title="At a glance">



</example>

None of it is code of the demo's own: the lists reorder live, the columns trade stops (one `group`),
a selection travels together (`selected`), <kbd value="Alt">



</kbd>

 turns a move into a copy (`clone`),
and the keyboard does all of it by slots. The demo renders the stops and passes a few options.

## What it is

A set of **composables** and one **provider** component. You render your own elements and hand
their template refs to the composables; the library takes care of the rest: pointer, touch and
keyboard input, finding the target, reordering, animating, auto-scrolling and telling screen
readers what happened.

```vue [Day.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
const listRef = useTemplateRef<HTMLElement>('list');
// `items` is the draft: it reorders while you drag. On drop, `day.stops` gets the new order.
const { items } = makeSortableList(listRef, { items: toRef(props.day, 'stops'), group: 'trip' });
</script>

<template>
  <ul ref="list">
    <StopCard v-for="stop in items" :key="stop.id" :stop="stop" />
  </ul>
</template>
```

It renders nothing of its own except a floating **overlay** — by default, a clone of the element
being dragged. Your markup and your styles stay yours: the library adds ARIA attributes, and a few
`data-dnd-*` attributes to style the states of a drag.

## What you get

- **Sortable lists and grids** that reorder live while you drag, vertical, horizontal or in a grid.
- **Lists that share items**: kanban boards, palettes that hand out copies, swaps, rules for what
goes where.
- **Trees** with nesting by a sideways drag or by hovering a row, depth limits and rules.
- **Multi-drag** with your own selection (Ctrl/Cmd-click, a rubber band): the block travels
together.
- **Drop zones** with accept rules, and drops you confirm, refuse or apply yourself.
- **Animations by default**: items slide to their new places, the drop lands on its slot, a cancel
flies back.
- **Accessibility**: keyboard drags by slots, live announcements, ARIA attributes.
- **Virtual lists** with TanStack Virtual or VueUse: thousands of rows.
- **Sensors and actions**: your own input devices, and drags scripted from code.
- **DevTools**: a tab with a live map of every list, a joystick and a log of each drag.

## How it is different

- **Your data stays yours until the drop.** You render a *draft* of your array. While you drag,
only the draft moves; on drop the library writes the new order into your ref, or hands you
`e.result` to apply yourself (stores, servers, undo).
- **No wrapper components.** Rows are your elements, with a ref and one call, so the components
of a UI kit (Nuxt UI, Vuetify, your own) drag as they are.
- **Animated by default, never in your way.** Reorders, landings and cancels animate out of the
box; turn them off, tune them, or hand them to GSAP or motion.
- **The keyboard is not an afterthought.** Every drag can be done with <kbd value="Space">



</kbd>

 and the
arrows, moves are announced, and focus comes back where it was.
- **One provider for the whole app.** Areas give parts of the page their own rules (an axis,
bounds, a grid, a longer press), so nested features don't need nested providers.
- **Input is pluggable.** Pointer and keyboard are sensors; write your own for a gamepad or a
voice command, or move items from code with `@vue-dnd-kit/actions`.

- In a list, an arrow toward another list of the same group moves the item there.
- In a free drag, <kbd value="Shift">



</kbd>

 makes the steps bigger. `makeDraggable(el, { keyboardMode: 'droppables' })`
makes the arrows jump between the targets that accept the item instead.
- A keyboard drag starts from the focused draggable, or its handle — never from a button or a
field inside it, so those keep their own keys.
- Keyboard drags scroll the item into view instead of auto-scrolling at the edges.
- After the drop, focus goes back to the item, even when its row was re-rendered in another
list.

### Other keys

```vue
<DnDProvider :keyboard="{ keys: { start: ['KeyD'], drop: ['KeyD', 'Enter'], cancel: ['Escape'] }, step: 10 }">
```

Bindings match `event.code` (`'Space'`, `'KeyD'`) or `event.key` (`'Enter'`). `step` is the
pixels per arrow press in free drags (25 by default). `:keyboard="false"` turns keyboard
drags off, and <kbd value="Escape">



</kbd>

 still cancels any drag. When you change the keys, change
the `screen-reader-instructions` too.

`attributes: false` on an item removes what the library had set, live. The panel reads the
attributes back: `aria-describedby` points to the provider's instructions, which a screen
reader reads after the item's name.

### Links and buttons that drag

`aria-roledescription` replaces the name of the role: a screen reader says "Inbox,
sortable" instead of "Inbox, button". For an element whose role matters, set your own; the
library leaves it alone:

```vue [Shortcut.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
makeSortableItem(el, {
  item: () => props.shortcut,
  // Enter follows the link: only Space picks it up.
  canDrag: (event) => !('key' in event && event.key === 'Enter'),
});
</script>

<template>
  <a ref="el" :href="shortcut.href" role="link" aria-roledescription="draggable link">
    {{ shortcut.title }}
  </a>
</template>
```

- A link keeps working: a click opens it, but the click that ends a drag never reaches it.
<kbd value="Enter">



</kbd>

 would start a drag, so `canDrag` turns that down and the browser follows
the link.
- A `<button>` keeps its click too, and the library adds neither `role` nor `tabindex`.
- Buttons, links and fields **inside** an item don't start pointer drags, so a row can hold
its own actions.

### Handles: make them real buttons

```vue [Track.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
import { useTemplateRef } from 'vue';
import { makeSortableItem } from '@vue-dnd-kit/core';

const props = defineProps<{ track: { id: string; title: string } }>();
const el = useTemplateRef<HTMLElement>('el');
makeSortableItem(el, { item: () => props.track, handle: '.grip' });
</script>

<template>
  <li ref="el" class="track">
    {{ track.title }}
    <button type="button" class="grip" :aria-label="`Drag ${track.title}`">⠿</button>
  </li>
</template>
```

With a `handle`, the attributes go on the handle, and keyboard drags start from it (the
**Archive** shortcut above). A `<button>` is focusable and a button already, so it needs no
`tabindex` or `role`. Give it an `aria-label`: a grip icon has no name of its own, and "Drag
Midnight Drive" says more than "button".

<tip>

The handle keeps the focus for the whole keyboard drag, while its row is the slot. Empty the
slot with `opacity: 0` rather than `visibility: hidden` or `display: none` on the handle: a
hidden element drops the focus. The library gives it back after the drop, but a screen reader
may say "body" in between.

</tip>

## Announcements

A live region in the provider speaks every pickup, move, drop and cancel. Sortable lists say
where the item is: *"Picked up item t2 at position 2 of 5 in list playlist."* Moves are
spoken once the drag has rested for 500 ms, so a fast pointer drag isn't read slot by slot.
The demo's panel logs every text the provider is given, including the moves a pointer drag
passes on its way.

The built-in texts are in English, and name things by their ids unless you give them a
`label`. Items, lists, trees and drop targets all take one:

```ts
makeSortableList(list, { items: tracks, label: 'Playlist' });
makeSortableItem(el, { item: () => props.track, label: () => props.track.title });
makeDroppable(bin, { label: 'Trash', onDrop });
```

*"Picked up Blue in Green at position 2 of 5 in Playlist."* The labels reach your own texts
and monitors too: `active.label`, `over.label`, each of `active.items`, and in the context
`position.label` and `partner.label`.

For another language, or other words, write the texts yourself, as the agenda does. Each
text gets the event and a `context`: the `position` the built-in text would speak (`list`,
`index` from 0, `length`, the list's `label`), and `count`, `copy` and a swap's `partner`.

```ts [index.vue]
const titleOf = (id: Key) => agenda.value.find((item) => item.id === id)?.title ?? String(id);

const announcements = computed<Partial<Announcements>>(() => {
  const t = LANGUAGES[lang.value]!;
  return {
    onDragStart: ({ active }, { position }) => position && t.start(titleOf(active.id), position.index + 1, position.length),
    onDragOver: ({ active }, { position }) => position && t.move(titleOf(active.id), position.index + 1, position.length),
    onDragEnd: ({ active }, { position }) => position && t.drop(titleOf(active.id), position.index + 1, position.length),
    onDragCancel: ({ active }, { position }) => position && t.cancel(titleOf(active.id), position.index + 1),
    onDragResume: ({ active }) => t.resume(titleOf(active.id)),
  };
});
```

```vue [index.vue]
<DnDProvider :announcements="announcements" :screen-reader-instructions="texts.instructions">
```

- A text replaces the event's announcement; `undefined` keeps the default; `''` says
nothing. Events you leave out keep their defaults, such as the positions of sortable lists.
- `screenReaderInstructions` is the text every draggable points to with `aria-describedby`.
Both props are reactive: the demo switches the language live.
- `:announcements="false"` silences the region, e.g. when you announce through your own.

<note>

For another language, give all five texts and the instructions: each one you leave out is
spoken in English, sortable positions included. Set the page's `lang` too, so the screen
reader picks the right voice.

</note>

## Moving without dragging

Some people can't drag at all. WCAG 2.5.7 asks for a way to move items with single
clicks. Use the arrows and the check on each row: they move the books without a drag, and
the focus stays where you are.

<example height="27.5rem" hint="Use the arrow buttons with the keyboard, or drag a grip" name="a11y-move-buttons">



</example>

A button changes the data; the list draws the move. With `animateChanges` on the list, the rows
slide as they do in a drag (and stay still for users who ask for reduced motion):

```ts [ReadingList.vue]
const { items } = makeSortableList(list, { id: 'reading', items: books, animateChanges: true });

// Buttons change the data, not a drag: the provider says nothing, so this region does.
const message = ref('');

const move = (from: number, to: number) => {
  const next = [...books.value];
  const [book] = next.splice(from, 1);
  next.splice(to, 0, book!);
  books.value = next;
  message.value = `${book!.title} moved to position ${to + 1} of ${next.length}.`;
};
```

```vue [ReadingList.vue]
<p class="status" role="status">{{ message }}</p>
```

### Keep the focus

Moving an element in the DOM takes the focus away from it, so the button that was just
pressed loses it. Give it back once the row has moved:

```ts [BookRow.vue]
const move = async (direction: 'up' | 'down') => {
  emit('move', direction === 'up' ? props.index - 1 : props.index + 1);
  await nextTick();
  // Back on the same button, or on the other one when this one is now disabled.
  const same = direction === 'up' ? up.value : down.value;
  const other = direction === 'up' ? down.value : up.value;
  (same?.disabled ? other : same)?.focus();
};
```

A row that goes away (the check marks a book as read) takes the focus with it: move it to
the next row, or the last one. Drags need none of this: the library puts the focus back on
the dropped item itself, even when it re-renders in another list.

<tip>

`@vue-dnd-kit/actions` turns each button into a real keyboard drag instead: `moveItem(id, { index })`
is announced, goes through `onBeforeDrop` and `onDrop`, animates, and keeps the focus on the
item. See [programmatic drags](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/sensors#programmatic-drags).

</tip>

## Touch

Touch drags start after a 200 ms long press. Moving more than 5 px first scrolls the page
instead, so lists stay scrollable. Tune both with the provider's `activation`, and draw a
long-press ring from `useDnD().activation.progress`: see
[the provider](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/provider#when-a-press-becomes-a-drag). A touch drag vibrates
briefly when it starts; `:haptics="false"` turns that off.

## Reduced motion

With `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, the library's own animations don't run: items jump
to their places while sorting, the overlay doesn't fly on drop, and `animateChanges` changes
appear at once. Your own animation functions still run, with `reducedMotion: true`, so you
decide: skip them, or keep a short fade. See [animations](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/animations).

---

- **Page:** Sortable lists
- **Source:** https://zizigy.github.io/vue-dnd-kit/docs/guides/sortable-lists
- **Description:** Lists, tab strips and grids that reorder while you drag — makeSortableList renders a draft, makeSortableItem makes the rows, and the drop writes the new order into your ref. Handles, a drop line, swaps.

<example height="25rem" hint="Drag a layer by its grip: the panel moves now, the artboard on drop" name="layers-panel">



</example>

## A list and its rows

A sortable list takes two components: the list, and its row.

```vue [LayersPanel.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
import { useTemplateRef } from 'vue';
import { makeSortableList } from '@vue-dnd-kit/core';
import LayerRow from './LayerRow.vue';

const layers = defineModel<Layer[]>({ required: true });
const list = useTemplateRef<HTMLElement>('list');
const { items } = makeSortableList(list, { items: layers });
</script>

<template>
  <ul ref="list">
    <LayerRow v-for="layer in items" :key="layer.id" :layer="layer" />
  </ul>
</template>
```

```vue [LayerRow.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
import { useTemplateRef } from 'vue';
import { makeSortableItem } from '@vue-dnd-kit/core';

const props = defineProps<{ layer: Layer }>();
const el = useTemplateRef<HTMLElement>('el');
makeSortableItem(el, { item: () => props.layer });
</script>

<template>
  <li ref="el">{{ layer.name }}</li>
</template>
```

The row registers with the list it is rendered in. A component may make several lists
(two columns, a list inside a list): each row joins the one whose element holds it, the
innermost for lists inside lists.

## The draft

`makeSortableList` returns `items`, a **draft** of your array. While you drag, the draft
reorders live: the dragged row takes its new slot, and the others slide out of the way.
Your array doesn't change until the drop. Then the library writes the new order into it.

The layers panel above shows both: the panel renders `items` and moves while you drag;
the artboard reads `layers`, the array itself, and restacks only when you let go.

- Render `items`, not your array. Rendering your array, nothing moves until the drop.
- The write happens after the list's `onDrop`. In `onDrop`, your array still holds the
old order and `e.result` the new one.
- `layers` is a regular ref (here a `defineModel`, and the write emits
`update:modelValue`), so the rest of your app sees the change like any other.

```ts
makeSortableList(list, {
  items: layers,
  onDrop: (e) => {
    console.log(e.from.index, '→', e.to.index, e.result.get(e.to.list));
  },
});
```

<tip>

A store, server state or immutable data? Pass a getter or a `computed` instead of a ref.
The library won't write a read-only source: call `e.preventDefault()` and apply `e.result`
yourself. See [controlled lists](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/shared-lists#controlled-lists).

</tip>

## Keys

Rows are keyed by their data, never by index or by an automatic id. By default the key is
`item.id`, or the item itself for strings and numbers.

```ts
// LayersPanel.vue: your items have another key
makeSortableList(list, { items: layers, getKey: (layer) => layer.uuid });

// LayerRow.vue: `item` is keyed with the list's getKey…
makeSortableItem(el, { item: () => props.layer });
// …or pass the key yourself
makeSortableItem(el, { id: () => props.layer.uuid });
```

- Use the same key in `v-for`: `:key="layer.uuid"`. With `:key="index"` the wrong rows
animate and their state jumps between rows.
- Keys must be unique among all the lists that exchange items.
- Pass `item` and `id` as getters, so a row stays in sync when its props change.

## Handles

By default the whole row starts a drag, except the buttons, inputs and other controls in
it: the eye and the lock of a layer stay plain buttons. Pass `handle` to drag by one part
only:

```vue [LayerRow.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
makeSortableItem(el, { item: () => props.layer, handle: '.grip' });
</script>

<template>
  <li ref="el">
    <button type="button" class="grip" :aria-label="`Move ${layer.name}`">⠿</button>
    {{ layer.name }}
  </li>
</template>
```

- `handle` is a selector inside the item, or an element ref.
- A mouse drag starts from the handle at once, without the usual 4 px. A press that
doesn't move is still a click: the handle can open a menu on `click`.
- The handle gets the drag's attributes (`role`, `tabindex`, `aria-*`), and keyboard
drags start from it.

Make the handle a `<button type="button">` with an `aria-label`: it is focusable as is,
and screen readers announce its label. A bare `<span>` with an icon also works (the
library gives it `tabindex="0"` and `role="button"`), but it has no meaningful name.

<note>

Touch drags start after a 200 ms long press, so the page can still scroll. To drag at once
from a handle, give the handle `touch-action: none` and the item
`activation: { touch: { distance: 4 } }`.

</note>

`strategy` says how the list is laid out, so the rows make room the right way:

A row of tabs is a horizontal list:

<example height="23rem" hint="Drag the tabs; close one, or open a new one" name="browser-tabs">



</example>

```ts [Browser.vue]
const { items } = makeSortableList(strip, {
  items: tabs,
  strategy: 'horizontal',
  axis: 'x',        // the tabs stay on their row
  animateChanges: true, // the buttons open and close tabs: slide the others then too
});
```

The tab's close button keeps working inside the draggable tab, and a click that ends a
drag doesn't select a tab. Rows slide on their own while you drag; `animateChanges` adds the same
for changes no drag made, here the buttons (see [animations](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/animations)).

A grid sorts in two dimensions, with tiles of any size:

<example height="31rem" hint="Drag a photo, the big one too" name="photo-grid">



</example>

```ts [PhotoGrid.vue]
const { items } = makeSortableList(grid, { items: photos, strategy: 'grid' });
```

```css
.grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 76px); grid-auto-rows: 76px; grid-auto-flow: dense; }
.wide { grid-column: span 2; }
.tall { grid-row: span 2; }
```

`grid-auto-flow: dense` keeps the grid packed when a big tile moves. Without it, the
grid leaves holes where a tile no longer fits, and grows a row.

## Lock the axis

```ts
makeSortableList(list, { items: layers, axis: 'y' });
```

`axis: 'y'` keeps the drag on the vertical axis, `'x'` on the horizontal one: the layers
and the tabs above use it. An item's own `axis` wins over its list's. To also keep the
drag inside the list, add the `restrictToParent` modifier. More in
[constraints](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/constraints).

## Style the slot

The dragged row stays in the list as the slot it will land in, and gets
`data-dnd-placeholder`. The default style fades it to 40%, with zero specificity, so any
rule of yours wins:

```css [LayerRow.vue]
.layer[data-dnd-placeholder] {
  opacity: 1;
  box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1.5px #42b883;
}

.layer[data-dnd-placeholder] > * {
  visibility: hidden;   /* an empty slot of the row's exact size */
}
```

`makeSortableItem` returns the same state as refs, plus a few more:

All of them take a getter or a ref, and apply to the next drag:

```ts [LayerRow.vue]
makeSortableItem(el, { item: () => props.layer, handle: '.grip', disabled: () => props.layer.locked });
```

A row that must stay first or last, whatever the others do, isn't an item at all: render
it outside the list. The Background layer of the panel sits below the `<ul>`.

## Show some of the items

A search box, a tag: `filter` shows the items it returns `true` for, and a drag sorts among
those. The others stay in your array, in their places:

<example height="27rem" hint="Pick a tag or search, then drag a task: the array keeps the hidden ones in place" name="filtered-list">



</example>

```ts [Backlog.vue]
const query = ref('');
const tag = ref<Tag | null>(null);

const { items } = makeSortableList(list, {
  items: tasks,
  filter: (task) => (!tag.value || task.tag === tag.value) && task.title.includes(query.value),
});
```

- `items` holds the matching items: render it as usual. The filter is reactive: typing in
the search box updates the list at once.
- The drop writes the whole array. Each hidden item stays right after the shown item it
followed; when that one is the one that moved, it stays after the nearest one before it
that didn't.
- `e.to.index` and the list's `activeIndex` count the shown items. `e.result` holds the
whole array, hidden items included.

<note>

A `computed` that filters your array and is passed as `items` works too, but it is read
only: you would apply `e.result` yourself and work out where the hidden items go. `filter`
does both.

</note>

## An insertion line

```ts [IssueTable.vue]
const { items, indicator } = makeSortableList(body, { items: issues, placeholder: 'indicator' });
```

```vue [IssueRow.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
const { indicator } = makeSortableItem(el, { item: () => props.issue });

<template>

.row.drop-before::before { content: ''; position: absolute; top: -1.5px; left: 6px; right: 6px; height: 2px; background: #42b883; }

```

- The keyboard moves the line, too.
- A drop outside every target cancels in this mode (`dropOutside: 'cancel'`), as the list
never showed another order.
- The overlay covers part of the row under it. Make it a little see-through, and the line
shows through: `[data-dnd-overlay] .row { opacity: 0.85 }`.

## Swap instead of shift

With `behavior: 'swap'`, the dragged item trades places with the one under it, and the
others stay put:

<example height="29rem" hint="Swap two people, across the columns too; try On drop" name="on-call">



</example>

```ts [Rotation.vue]
const { items } = makeSortableList(list, {
  id: props.column.id,
  items: toRef(props.column, 'people'),
  group: 'rotation',
  behavior: 'swap',
  placeholder: () => props.placeholder,   // 'item' (live) or 'indicator' (on drop)
  onDrop: (e) => {
    if (e.partner) emit('swap', `${e.items[0]?.name} ⇄ ${e.partner.item.name}`);
  },
});
```

- **Live** (`placeholder: 'item'`, default): the swap shows while you drag. Moving back,
or off the list, undoes it.
- **On drop** (`placeholder: 'indicator'`): nothing moves until the drop. The indicator
marks the item the drop exchanges with, `side: 'swap'`: outline that item instead of
drawing a line. The arrows move the mark from item to item; back on the dragged item,
there is none.

```vue [PersonCell.vue]
<li ref="el" :class="{ target: indicator?.side === 'swap' }">…</li>
```

The drop event has `mode: 'swap'` and `partner`, the item it traded with: its `key`,
`item`, and its own `from` and `to`. Two lists of one group swap between them when both
have `behavior: 'swap'`, as the two columns do. The hovered item then moves into the
other list, so it must be allowed out (`group.pull`) and in (`group.put`): see
[lists that share items](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/shared-lists). A multi-drag sorts instead of
swapping.

## Keyboard

Focus a row, or its handle, and press <kbd value="Space">



</kbd>

 or <kbd value="Enter">



</kbd>

 to pick
it up. The arrows along the list move it by one slot, in grids up and down go to the next
row, and the arrows across the list move it to the next list of its group. Past the end of
a list, the arrow goes on into the next list that way (lists stacked one above another),
else onto a drop target there, a trash zone. Press
<kbd value="Space">



</kbd>

 or <kbd value="Enter">



</kbd>

 again to drop, <kbd value="Escape">



</kbd>

 to put it
back. Every demo on this page works that way. The screen reader texts are in
[accessibility](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/accessibility).

## Animations

Rows slide to their new places while you drag, and the dropped row lands on its slot. The
list itself grows or shrinks to its new size as rows come in and leave (`animateSize`). That
is on by default and needs no code. Don't wrap rows in `<TransitionGroup>`: moves would
animate twice. Don't put a CSS `transition` on the rows' `transform` either. For changes
no drag made (adding, removing, shuffling), turn on the list's `animateChanges` option, as the
tabs do. See [animations](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/animations).

The full option list is in the [makeSortableList](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/api/make-sortable-list) and
[makeSortableItem](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/api/make-sortable-item) API.

---

- **Page:** Migrating from v2
- **Source:** https://zizigy.github.io/vue-dnd-kit/docs/getting-started/migrating-from-v2
- **Description:** Move a v2 app to v3 — what changed and why, the upgrade, a map from every v2 API to its v3 replacement, before-and-after code for the common cases, and the pitfalls.

v3 is a rewrite of v2. The model stays: one provider, and composables you call on your own
elements. But most names and options changed, sorting moved into the library, and the drop
handler you wrote for each list goes away. This page maps each part of v2 to v3, then shows
the common cases before and after.

## What changed

- **Sorting is built in.** In v2 a list was a drop zone, its rows were draggables with an
`[index, items]` payload, and you sorted in `onDrop` with `e.helpers.suggestSort()`. In v3,
`makeSortableList` and `makeSortableItem` do it: the list renders a **draft** of your array
that reorders while you drag, and the drop writes the new array into your ref. Most v2 drop
handlers are deleted, not ported.
- **Things move by themselves.** Rows slide to their new places (FLIP), the overlay lands on
its slot on drop and flies back on cancel. `<TransitionGroup>` goes away.
- **Still one package.** `@vue-dnd-kit/core` holds lists, trees, multi-drag, modifiers,
sensors and the collision functions. The Nuxt module stays; `@vue-dnd-kit/actions`
(programmatic drags) and `@vue-dnd-kit/devtools` are new and optional.
- **A real overlay.** It is teleported to `body` and shows a deep clone, sized to the slot it
will land in. Overlay components get the drag as props instead of reading the provider's
internals.
- **Ids, not elements.** The selection, the events and the drag state are keyed by ids from
your data. There are no maps of DOM elements to read.
- **Types and accept rules** replace `groups` for plain draggables and targets. Lists trade
items by `group` name.
- **Decisions before the drop.** `onBeforeDrop` accepts, refuses, keeps the drag going or
takes some of the items. `onDrop` only applies.
- **Sensors.** Pointer and keyboard input are sensors. Activation is set per pointer kind,
and touch drags start with a long press, so lists keep scrolling under a finger.
- **Areas.** `makeDragArea` replaces `makeConstraintArea` and `makeAutoScroll`, and
auto-scroll works in every scroll container without code.
- **Accessibility is on by default**: ARIA attributes, focus that comes back after the drop,
and screen reader announcements.

## Upgrade

<code-group>

```bash [npm]
npm i @vue-dnd-kit/core@^3
```

```bash [yarn]
yarn add @vue-dnd-kit/core@^3
```

```bash [pnpm]
pnpm add @vue-dnd-kit/core@^3
```

```bash [bun]
bun add @vue-dnd-kit/core@^3
```

- An app that has `"@vue-dnd-kit/core": "^2…"` in its `package.json` stays on v2 until the
range says `^3`.
- Vue **3.5** or newer. v2 had no dependencies; v3 has one, `@vueuse/core` (14 or 15).
- Browsers: Chrome and Edge 104+, Safari 15.4+, Firefox 104+.
- v2 and v3 share a package name, so an app moves to v3 in one go. There is no
compatibility layer. The v2 docs stay available from the version menu at the top of the
page.

A good order of work:

1. Upgrade the packages and rename the provider's props ([below](#the-provider)).
2. Turn each sortable list into `makeSortableList` and `makeSortableItem`, and delete its drop
handler.
3. Port the plain draggables and drop zones.
4. Port custom previews to overlay components or the provider's `#overlay` slot.
5. Replace `makeConstraintArea` and `makeAutoScroll` with `makeDragArea`, or with nothing.
6. Delete the v2 workarounds: `tabindex` and `aria-grabbed` on draggables, `touch-action: none`
on whole items, `<TransitionGroup>` around rows, `markRaw` around preview components.

### Groups

v2 had one `groups` option for everything. v3 splits it in two:

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      v2
    </th>
    
    <th>
      v3
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        makeDraggable(el, { groups: ['dev'] })
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        makeDraggable(el, { type: 'dev' })
      </code>
      
      .
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        makeDroppable(el, { groups: ['dev'] })
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        makeDroppable(el, { accept: 'dev' })
      </code>
      
      .
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        groups: ['dev', 'ops']
      </code>
      
       on a zone
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        accept: ['dev', 'ops']
      </code>
      
      , or a function: <code>
        ({ active, items, types }) => boolean
      </code>
      
      .
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        groups: []
      </code>
      
      , or none
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        type
      </code>
      
       or <code>
        accept
      </code>
      
       left out. The v2 rules hold: an untyped draggable fits any rule, and a target without <code>
        accept
      </code>
      
       takes everything.
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        groupMatch: 'every'
      </code>
      
      , <code>
        'some'
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        acceptMode: 'all'
      </code>
      
      , <code>
        'some'
      </code>
      
      .
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        groups
      </code>
      
       on a list zone and its rows
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        group: 'board'
      </code>
      
       on <code>
        makeSortableList
      </code>
      
      . <code>
        group: { name, pull, put }
      </code>
      
       says what may leave and enter.
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        groups
      </code>
      
       on <code>
        makeSelectionArea
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        accept
      </code>
      
      .
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

A list without `group` is a group of its own and trades with no other list. In v2, a zone
without groups took everything. See [which drags a target takes](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/drag-and-drop#which-drags-a-target-takes).

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>

    </th>

### Events and drop decisions

<table>

    </th>
    
    <th>
      v3
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

  <tr>
    <td>

        events.onSelfDragStart
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        useDnDMonitor({ onDragStart })
      </code>
      
      , checking <code>
        active.ids
      </code>
      
      . For a class, <code>
        isDragging
      </code>
      
       is enough.
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        onSelfDragMove
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The monitor's <code>
        onDragMove
      </code>
      
      .
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        onSelfDragEnd
      </code>
      
      , dropped or cancelled
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The monitor's <code>
        onDragEnd
      </code>
      
       (a drop) and <code>
        onDragCancel
      </code>
      
      . <code>
        onDragSettle
      </code>
      
       hears both, once the overlay has landed.
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>

      </code>

  </tr>
  
  <tr>

      </code>

      </code>
      
      , and its <code>
        onDragStart
      </code>
      
      … for drags over it
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        makeDroppable
      </code>
      
       on the element: <code>
        onDragEnter
      </code>
      
      , <code>
        onDragLeave
      </code>
      
      . Rows of a list need nothing.
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      Droppable <code>
        events.onEnter
      </code>
      
      , <code>
        onLeave
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        onDragEnter
      </code>
      
      , <code>
        onDragLeave
      </code>
      
      .
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      Droppable <code>
        events.onDrop
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        onBeforeDrop
      </code>
      
       decides, then <code>
        onDrop
      </code>
      
       applies. <code>
        onDrop
      </code>
      
       is synchronous, and what it returns is ignored.
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      Droppable <code>
        events.onValidate
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        onBeforeDrop
      </code>
      
      , with <code>
        acceptMode: 'some'
      </code>
      
      .
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      —
    </td>
    
    <td>
      New: the provider's <code>
        @drag-start
      </code>
      
       … <code>
        @drag-settle
      </code>
      
      , and the monitor's <code>
        onDragOver
      </code>
      
      , <code>
        onBeforeDrop
      </code>
      
       and <code>
        onDragResume
      </code>
      
      .
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

A v2 `onDrop` could return a value, or a promise of one, to decide the drop. In v3 that is the
job of `onBeforeDrop`, on lists, trees, drop targets and monitors:

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      v2 <code>
        onDrop
      </code>
      
       returns
    </th>
    
    <th>
      v3 <code>
        onBeforeDrop
      </code>
      
       returns
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      Nothing, or <code>
        true
      </code>
      
      : the drop goes through
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        'accept'
      </code>
      
      , <code>
        true
      </code>
      
       or nothing.
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        false
      </code>
      
      : this drop is declined, the drag stays active
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        'continue'
      </code>
      
      . <strong>
        <code>
          false
        </code>
        
         now refuses the drop.
      </strong>
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      A rejected promise, or a throw: the drag is cancelled
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        'reject'
      </code>
      
       or <code>
        false
      </code>
      
      . A throw rejects too.
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      A promise; meanwhile <code>
        state
      </code>
      
       is <code>
        'pending'
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      A promise; meanwhile <code>
        status
      </code>
      
       is <code>
        'dropping'
      </code>
      
       and the overlay waits with <code>
        data-dnd-overlay="dropping"
      </code>
      
      .
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        onValidate
      </code>
      
       returns <code>
        IDragItem[]
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      An array of ids: only those drop, the others fly back.
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

Monitors answer first, then the target. Then the target's `onDrop` runs, a list writes its
new arrays, and `onDragEnd` follows. More in [deciding a drop](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/drop-decisions)
and the [events API](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/api/events).
