    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      Pen
    </td>
    
    <td>
      After moving 4 px.
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      Touch
    </td>
    
    <td>
      After a 200 ms press. Moving more than 5 px first gives up, so the page scrolls instead.
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

### Where to set them

Per pointer kind — `mouse`, `touch`, `pen` — on the provider, a drag area or the item. For each
kind, the item's own wins, then its area's, then the provider's:

```vue
<DnDProvider :activation="{ mouse: { distance: 8 }, touch: { delay: 250, tolerance: 5 } }">
```

```ts
// Inbox.vue: the rules of every drag that starts inside the panel.
makeDragArea(panel, { activation: () => MODES[mode.value].activation });

// One item: a longer press by touch, the area's rule for the mouse.
makeSortableItem(el, { item: () => props.task, activation: { touch: { delay: 400, tolerance: 8 } } });
```

The options are read when a press starts, so a getter or a ref switches them live, as the demo does.
Keyboard drags start at once. [A sensor of your own](#a-sensor-of-your-own) asks for its own
constraint, or for the one configured for a pointer kind.

### A long-press ring

While a press waits, `useDnD().status` is `'activating'` and `activation.progress` goes from 0 to
1 — by time with `delay`, by the distance moved with `distance`. The demo draws a ring where the
press started:

```vue [Inbox.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
const { status, activation } = useDnD();
</script>

<template>
  <svg v-if="status === 'activating'" class="ring" viewBox="0 0 40 40">
    <circle cx="20" cy="20" r="17" pathLength="1" :stroke-dasharray="`${activation.progress.value} 1`" />
  </svg>
</template>
```

Give the ring `pointer-events: none`: it sits under the pointer, and the drag hit-tests what is
there. A press that gives up — moved past its `tolerance`, or let go too early — takes `status`
straight back to `'idle'`.

### Handles start at once

With a `handle`, only the handle starts a drag, and a mouse press on it drags at once: grabbing a
grip leaves nothing to tell apart. A press released where it started is still a click, so the
grip can open a menu on `click` (the pointer is captured only once it moves). A touch still waits for its long press, unless the handle can't
scroll the page. Give it `touch-action: none` and the item a short distance:

```ts [Message.vue]
makeSortableItem(el, {
  item: () => props.chat,
  handle: '.grip',
  // The grip has `touch-action: none`: a touch on it can't scroll, so it drags after 4 px.
  activation: { touch: { distance: 4 } },
});
```

A mouse constraint set on the item, its area or the provider applies to handles too. Make the
grip a `<button>`, as the demo does: it takes the focus, so a keyboard drag starts from it
too.

## Only some presses

`canDrag` is one more gate on draggables and sortable items. It gets the input event and answers
`true` or `false` for this press. Here pointer drags need <kbd value="Shift">



</kbd>

; the keyboard drags
as usual:

<example height="28rem" hint="Drag a row with and without Shift; tick a box, pick an owner" name="can-drag">



</example>

```ts [Task.vue]
makeSortableItem(el, {
  item: () => props.task,
  // Never: the row is locked (and says so to screen readers with aria-disabled).
  disabled: () => !!props.task.locked,
  // Per press: pointer drags only with Shift held; the keyboard as usual.
  canDrag: (event) => {
    if (!props.shiftOnly || event instanceof KeyboardEvent || event.shiftKey) return true;
    emit('refused');
    return false;
  },
});
```

`canDrag` is asked before the activation constraint, with the `pointerdown` or `keydown`. A pointer
type is one more rule it can make:

```ts
// Mouse and pen drag; a touch on the row always scrolls the page.
canDrag: (event) => !(event instanceof PointerEvent && event.pointerType === 'touch'),
```

Interactive children — buttons, inputs, checkboxes, editable fields — never start a pointer drag,
so they keep working inside a draggable, as the checkbox and the owner menu in the demo do. With a
`handle`, only the handle starts one.

## A sensor of your own

A gamepad, an on-screen joystick, voice commands: anything that can point at an item and move can
drive a drag. This gamepad is a sensor. Hold <kbd value="A">



</kbd>

 over a hero to pick it up, steer with
the pad, <kbd value="A">



</kbd>

 again drops, <kbd value="B">



</kbd>

 cancels. The mouse and the keyboard still work
next to it:

<example height="30rem" hint="Hold A over a hero, then hold an arrow: the hero moves through the list" name="joystick">



</example>

`defineSensor` gives the sensor its name and a `setup` that receives the provider's side, once per
provider:

```ts [joystick.ts]
const sensor = defineSensor({
  name: 'joystick',
  // Once per provider, in the browser. The cleanup runs when the provider unmounts.
  setup(ctx) {
    context = ctx;
    return () => {
      context = null;
      drag = null;
    };
  },
});
```

A press asks the provider for a drag with `activate()`. The target is checked like a real press:
it must be a draggable of this provider, not disabled, and not a button inside one:

```ts [joystick.ts]
/** A goes down: drops a running drag, or starts a hold over what is under the cursor. */
const press = () => {
  if (drag?.state === 'dragging') return void drag.drop();
  const at = point();
  const target = document.elementFromPoint(at.x, at.y);
  if (!target || !context) return;
  drag = context.activate({
    target, // checked like a real press: a draggable of this provider, not disabled
    point: at,
    type: 'pointer', // follows points: lists sort under it, containers auto-scroll
    activation: { delay: 300 }, // `useDnD().activation.progress` runs meanwhile
    onEnd: (ended) => {
      if (drag === ended) drag = null;
    },
  }); // null: nothing to drag there
};
```

Then the drag moves with the pad, and A or B end it:

```ts [joystick.ts]
const move = (dx: number, dy: number) => {
  cursor.value = { x: cursor.value.x + dx, y: cursor.value.y + dy }; // clamped in the demo
  drag?.move(point()); // pending: checks the tolerance; dragging: moves
};

const release = () => {
  if (drag?.state === 'pending') drag.cancel(); // A let go before the hold is over
};

const cancel = () => drag?.cancel();
```

Add the sensor to the provider's `sensors`, as the demo does, or run it for as long as a component
lives with `useSensor(joystick.sensor)`. Points are in viewport coordinates: the demo keeps its
cursor in the stage's coordinates, so it scrolls with the page, and converts it in `point()`.

Calls that no longer apply — a move after the end, a second `drop()` — are ignored. Full types:
[Sensors](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/api/sensors).

<tip>

To wrap a built-in sensor, run its `setup` with a context of your own. Make it with
`Object.create(context, { activate: { value: myActivate } })` rather than a spread, so the live
getters (`status`, `drag`, `props`) keep working.

</tip>

## Programmatic drags

`@vue-dnd-kit/actions` moves items from code: "Move up" buttons, menus, keyboard shortcuts, undo,
onboarding tours, tests. It is built on the public sensor API, and its drags are real ones:
announced and animated, through `onBeforeDrop`, `onDrop`, `e.result` and `preventDefault()`, under
the provider's rules (one drag at a time, disabled items, `accept` and `group.put`).

<example height="31.5rem" hint="Hover a track for its arrows, shuffle, or play the scripted drag" name="actions">



</example>

```bash
npm i @vue-dnd-kit/actions
```

### moveItem: one call, one move

```ts
import { useDnDActions } from '@vue-dnd-kit/actions';

const { moveItem } = useDnDActions(); // in setup, under a provider

await moveItem('card-1', { index: 0 }); // to the top of its list
await moveItem('card-1', { list: 'done' }); // to the end of another list
await moveItem('card-1', { list: 'done', index: 2 }); // to a place in another list
```

- `list` is a sortable list's `id`. Without it, the item stays in its list.
- `index` is where the item ends up, counted without the item itself, and clamped to the list.
Without it, the item goes to the end.
- It resolves `true` when the drop went through, `false` when the item isn't rendered or is
disabled, no list takes it there, or the drop was refused.
- Calls queue: each waits until the provider is idle, so a quick second click isn't lost. The
shuffle in the demo is five calls in a row.
- It runs as a keyboard drag, so it is announced and the focus stays on the item.
- Lists only: tree positions also have a depth.

See [Accessibility](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/accessibility#moving-without-dragging) for a row with move buttons.

### startDrag: a scripted drag

```ts
const { startDrag } = useDnDActions();

const drag = startDrag('card-1'); // null when it can't start now
if (drag) {
  await drag.moveTo(document.querySelector('#trash')!); // onto an element
  await drag.moveTo({ x: 400, y: 120 }); // to a point, in viewport coordinates
  await drag.moveTo({ list: 'done', index: 2 }); // to a list position
  await drag.drop(); // true when the drop went through; or drag.cancel()
}
```

`moveTo` resolves once the move has rendered, `drop` once the drop has landed. The demo's
"Play a scripted drag" glides the last track up in small `moveTo` steps, then drops it at the top.
`startDrag(id, { from: { x, y } })` picks the item up at a point instead of its center.

### Hand a drag to the keyboard

`startDrag(id, { type: 'keyboard' })` lifts the item as a keyboard drag. Your code can move it with
`await drag.step('down')`, or leave it to the user: the keyboard sensor drives every keyboard drag,
whoever started it. That makes a "Move" menu item:

<example height="26rem" hint="Open a row's menu: arrow keys, or send it to the other week" name="move-menu">



</example>

```ts [Row.vue]
const { moveItem, startDrag } = useDnDActions();

// One move in one call: picked up, put there and dropped, announced and animated.
const toOther = () => moveItem(props.task.id, { list: props.other.id, index: 0 });
// A keyboard drag, handed to the arrow keys: Space or Enter drops, Escape cancels.
const withKeys = () => {
  el.value?.focus();
  startDrag(props.task.id, { type: 'keyboard' });
};
```

The arrows move the row by slots, <kbd value="ArrowLeft">



</kbd>

 and <kbd value="ArrowRight">



</kbd>

 to the
other week (the lists share a `group`). When the drag ends, the focus goes back to the row. The
key hints under the board light up while `useDnD().active.value?.sensor` is `'keyboard'`.

### Outside components

`useDnDActions()` runs one sensor, named `actions`, in the provider above. To drive a provider from
a store or a test harness, or under a name of your own, create the actions in a sensor you run
yourself:

```ts
import { defineSensor } from '@vue-dnd-kit/core';
import { createDnDActions, type DnDActions } from '@vue-dnd-kit/actions';

export let tour: DnDActions | undefined;
export const tourSensor = defineSensor({
  name: 'tour',
  setup: (context) => void (tour = createDnDActions(context)),
});
```

```vue
<DnDProvider :sensors="[pointerSensor, keyboardSensor, tourSensor]">
```

Then `await tour?.moveItem('card-1', { list: 'done' })` from anywhere. During server rendering
nothing drags: `moveItem` resolves `false` and `startDrag` returns `null`.

---

- **Page:** makeDragArea
- **Source:** https://zizigy.github.io/vue-dnd-kit/docs/api/make-drag-area
- **Description:** Rules for the drags that start inside an element — an axis, bounds, a grid, auto-scroll, activation — under one app-wide provider.

<api-signature name="makeDragArea">



</api-signature>

```ts

makeDragArea(board, { restrictToArea: true, modifiers: [snapToGrid(24)] });
```

Inner areas inherit `disabled`; every other rule comes from the closest area. See
[Axes, bounds and grids](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/constraints).

The chips inside the area follow its rules; the one outside it drags freely.

## useDnD

<api-signature name="useDnD">



</api-signature>

```ts
const { status, active, over, selection, cancel } = useDnD();
const dragging = computed(() => status.value === 'dragging');
```

The state of the provider's drag, reactive. `active` and `over` are cleared as soon as the drop
is decided, while the overlay still lands. `addWindow(popup)` lets the provider work in another
window of the app (see [the provider guide](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/provider#other-windows-of-the-app)).

## Modifiers

```ts
import { restrictToParent, snapToGrid } from '@vue-dnd-kit/core';

makeSortableList(list, { items, modifiers: [restrictToParent] });
makeDragArea(board, { modifiers: [snapToGrid({ x: 24, y: 24, smooth: true })] });
```

A modifier takes the drag's offset and returns a new one. They run in order: the provider's
`modifiers`, a drag area's, the draggable's own (or its list's), then the area's bounds
(`restrictToArea`), and the `axis` lock last. See [Axes, bounds and grids](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/constraints).

<api-signature names="restrictToVerticalAxis, restrictToHorizontalAxis, restrictToWindowEdges, restrictToParent, restrictToElement, restrictToFirstScrollableAncestor, snapToGrid, snapCenterToCursor">

## DragPreview

<api-signature name="DragPreview">



</api-signature>

```vue [StackOverlay.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
import { DragPreview, type DragItem } from '@vue-dnd-kit/core';

defineProps<{ items: DragItem[] }>();
</script>

<template>
  <div class="stack">
    <DragPreview v-for="item in items.slice(0, 3)" :id="item.id" :key="item.id" />
  </div>
</template>
```

Clones are taken at pickup, of the grabbed item and of the others next to it in drop order,
as many as the provider's `overlayPreviews` (5 by default). For any other item `DragPreview`
renders its default slot, or nothing. On drop each preview flies to its own item; dropped
into a zone (a folder, a trash can), the previews go in one after another. See
[the overlay guide](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/overlay).

---

- **Page:** DnDProvider
- **Source:** https://zizigy.github.io/vue-dnd-kit/docs/api/dnd-provider
- **Description:** The component that owns the drag — input, the overlay, the selection, auto-scroll and the live region — for everything rendered inside it.

<api-signature name="DnDProvider">



</api-signature>

```vue [App.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
import { DnDProvider } from '@vue-dnd-kit/core';
</script>

<template>
  <DnDProvider :animation="{ duration: 200 }" @drag-end="save">
    <RouterView />
    <template #overlay="{ items, over, accepted }">
      <!-- optional: a custom overlay for every drag -->
    </template>
  </DnDProvider>
</template>
```

Every composable must run in a component rendered **inside** a provider. One provider for the
whole app is the goal: parts of the page get their own rules with
[`makeDragArea`](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/api/make-drag-area). See [the provider guide](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/provider).

Most props are read when the provider needs them: change one, and the next drag uses it.

<example height="37rem" hint="Switch a prop, then drag a task: by mouse, held, with Alt or Shift, or with Space on a focused task" name="api-provider-props">



</example>

### Where the overlay renders

`overlayTo` moves the overlay out of `body`: into a modal `<dialog>`, which sits above
everything else on the page. Turn the switch off, and the rows you drag vanish under the
dialog. The [overlay guide](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/overlay#where-it-renders-overlayto) explains when
it is needed.

<example height="22rem" hint="Open the dialog and drag a column; then turn the switch off and drag again" name="overlay-dialog">



</example>

- **Page:** Animations

- **Description:** The options and hooks of the animations — sorting, the drop, and changes no drag made.

The provider's `animation` (layout moves while sorting), `dropAnimation` (the overlay landing)
and `animateChanges` (data changes no drag made) take `false`, options, or your own function — for

[Animations](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/animations).

<DnDProvider :animation="{ duration: 180, easing: 'ease-out' }" :drop-animation="false" />

---

- **Page:** Data table
- **Source:** https://zizigy.github.io/vue-dnd-kit/docs/examples/data-table
- **Description:** A Nuxt UI table of 2,000 tasks, virtualized and searchable, sorted by dragging its rows by their grips.

<example height="34rem" hint="Drag a task by its grip; search, then drag: the hidden tasks keep their places" name="ui-table" title="Data table">



</example>

Nuxt UI's `UTable` renders the table, its rows and its virtualizer: only the rows on screen are in
the DOM. Vue DnD Kit sorts them. The table is the library's as it comes, with its slots and its
`ui` classes; nothing of it is rewritten.

## What to look at

- **TaskTable.vue**: the sortable list is the table's `<tbody>`, found through the `tableRef`
that `UTable` exposes. The table gets the list's draft as its `data`, so the rows move while you
drag, and `get-row-id` keys them by task, as the list does. `axis: 'y'` keeps the drag in its
column, and `restrictToFirstScrollableAncestor` inside the table: its scroller is the first
scrollable element around the rows. Expand the demo: the table fills the screen.
- **RowGrip.vue**: `UTable` renders the rows, so no component of yours is a row. The grip in the
first cell (the `#grip-cell` slot) makes the row around it the item, and is its handle.
- **The search** is the list's `filter`: the table shows the matching tasks, and a drop writes
the whole array back, the hidden tasks where they were.
- **tasks.ts**: 2,000 tasks in a `shallowRef`: the library never looks inside them.

## A row the table renders

The grip calls `makeSortableItem` with a getter for the row: the `<tr>` around it, once it is
rendered. As the handle, the grip takes the focus and the ARIA attributes, and the rest of the
row stays free for clicks and text selection.

```ts [RowGrip.vue]
const grip = useTemplateRef<HTMLElement>('grip');
makeSortableItem(() => grip.value?.closest('tr') ?? null, {
  id: () => props.task.id,
  handle: grip,
  label: () => props.task.title,
});
```

```vue [TaskTable.vue]
<UTable ref="table" :data="items" :get-row-id="(task: Task) => task.id" …>
  <template #grip-cell="{ row }">
    <RowGrip :task="row.original" />
  </template>
</UTable>
```

The overlay is the library's copy of the row, in a table of its own with the cells' widths. A
table row draws no shadow, so the provider's `overlay-class` gives the overlay's content one,
with the table's background and a ring. The row's `ui` classes tint its place while it travels
(`data-[dnd-placeholder]:bg-primary/5`).

```vue [index.vue]
<DnDProvider overlay-class="overflow-hidden rounded-md bg-default shadow-xl ring ring-accented">
  <TaskTable />
</DnDProvider>
```

## Virtualized rows

`virtualize` gives the table TanStack Virtual: the rows on screen and 8 more around them
(`overscan`) are rendered, between two spacer rows.

```vue [TaskTable.vue]
<UTable
  :data="items"
  :watch-options="{ deep: false }"
  :virtualize="{ estimateSize: 45, overscan: 8, onChange: () => captureLayout() }"
  class="min-h-0 flex-1"
/>
```

- `estimateSize` is a first guess: the virtualizer measures each row as it renders. A
measurement moves the rows below it, and `onChange` calls the list's `captureLayout()`, so the
library animates that move during a drag instead of letting it jump.
- The table is the scroller, and the row in hand stays inside it: near its top or bottom edge
a drag scrolls it, and new rows render as they come into view.
- The draft is a new array after every move, so the table needn't watch inside it
(`deep: false`).
- Scroll far from the row you hold, and it leaves the rendered range and unmounts. The drag goes
on: the overlay still shows it, and it lands where the draft puts it. A virtual list of your own
can keep it mounted with `rangeExtractor` (see [Virtual lists](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/virtual-lists#tanstack-virtual)).
A table lays its rows out between spacer rows, where a row rendered far from the others would
push them aside, so this one lets it go.

## Search, then drag

```ts [TaskTable.vue]
const { items, captureLayout } = makeSortableList(() => table.value?.tableRef?.tBodies[0] ?? null, {
  items: tasks,
  filter: (task) => {
    const text = query.value.trim().toLowerCase();
    return !text || `${task.id} ${task.title} ${task.assignee}`.toLowerCase().includes(text);
  },
  axis: 'y',
  modifiers: [restrictToFirstScrollableAncestor],
  label: 'Tasks',
});
```

Search "Mia", move one of her tasks above another, then clear the search: her tasks are in the
new order, and every other task is where it was. The drop's `e.to.index` counts the rows shown;
`e.result` holds the whole array.

<tip>

**Other UI libraries.** Nuxt UI renders plain elements and passes your classes and attributes on,
as the Reka UI primitives it is built on do: a ref, a slot and a class are all it takes. In other
libraries a table renders its rows too, and the same recipe works:

- **The row.** A slot that renders the whole row (Vuetify's `#item`, Quasar's `#body`) gives you
its element: make it the item. Where you only get cells (a PrimeVue `Column`'s `#body`, an
Element Plus column's default slot, Naive UI's `render`), put a grip in one and make its
`closest('tr')` the item, as here.
- **The list.** The `<tbody>` inside the table's root element: a template ref on the table gives
you the component, and its `$el` the element.
- **The keys and the data.** Key the rows by your id (`item-value`, `row-key`, `dataKey`) and give
the table the list's draft as its data.
- **Its own ordering off.** Leave out the table's own row reordering and its column sorting: the
order is the list's.
- **Virtual tables** place their rows between spacers or in absolute boxes: both work, and a drag
survives its row unmounting.

</tip>

<note>

The StackBlitz button opens the files in a Vite project set up for Nuxt UI, as its docs do it for
Vue: the `@nuxt/ui/vite` plugin, Tailwind CSS, and `UApp` around the example. In a Nuxt app with
the `@nuxt/ui` module, copy the folder and render `index.vue` on a page.

</note>

Tab to a task's grip and press <kbd value="Space">



</kbd>

 to pick the row up. <kbd value="ArrowUp">



</kbd>

 and
<kbd value="ArrowDown">



</kbd>

 move it, <kbd value="Space">



</kbd>

 drops it, <kbd value="Escape">



</kbd>

 puts it back.
The rows have a `label`, and the list too: screen readers hear "Fix the login form dropped at
position 3 of 2000 in Tasks.", not keys.

- **Page:** Week calendar
- **Source:** https://zizigy.github.io/vue-dnd-kit/docs/examples/calendar
- **Description:** A week planner — events moved across days and quarters of an hour, stretched by their edges, drawn on empty time, made all day, planned from a task list, with undo.

<example height="44rem" hint="Move or stretch an event, or draw one on empty time" name="calendar" title="Week calendar">



</example>

## What to look at

- **EventBlock.vue**: an event in the hours is a plain draggable whose overlay,
**EventOverlay.vue**, says where it would land: "Wed 10:30 – 11:15". Overlapping events go side
by side (`layoutDay` in `placement.ts`).
- **Edge.vue**: the top and bottom edges of an event are draggables of their own. Drag one and
the event stretches, a quarter of an hour at a time.
- **DayColumn.vue**: each day's hours are a drop target, and under its events lies a draggable
too: press empty time and drag to draw a new event, then type its title.
- **AllDayCell.vue** and **Tasks.vue**: drop an event on a day's all-day cell and it loses its
time; drop it on the task list and it loses its day. Tasks (**EventChip.vue**) drag into the
week, and keep their length.
- **Week.vue**: the drag area of the hours and their own modifier, the keyboard moves, the line
of the current time.
- **calendar.ts**: the events and an undo history. Every change goes through one function, and
the toast offers to take it back.

Expand the example: with room for it, a side panel shows the month, the calendars to show or hide,
and the tasks as a list. On a phone the week becomes three days, and a long press drags.

## One answer for every drop

What a drop would do is asked in four places: the overlay's label, the ghost a task shows in the
day under it, what screen readers hear, and the drop itself. They all call `placeOf`, so they
never disagree. Each drop target carries what it is in its `data`, and `position` is where the
dragged box is inside it: its top is the time.

```ts [placement.ts]
export function placeOf(event: CalendarEvent, over: Over | null, position: Coordinates | null): Place | null {
  const target = over?.accepted ? (over.data as Target) : null;
  if (!target) return null;
  if (target.kind === 'tasks') return { day: null, start: null };
  if (target.kind === 'all-day') return { day: target.day, start: null };
  if (!position) return null;
  return { day: target.day, start: clamp(minutesAt(position.y), 0, DAY_MINUTES - event.duration) };
}
```

The overlay reads it live, from `useDnD().position`, and keeps its last answer while it lands:

```ts [EventOverlay.vue]
const { position } = useDnD();
const place = shallowRef(placeOf(event.value, props.over, position.value));
watchEffect(() => {
  if (props.status === 'dragging') place.value = placeOf(event.value, props.over, position.value);
});
```

An event keeps its id, its `data` and its overlay wherever it is: a block in the hours, a chip all
day or among the tasks. Dropped somewhere else, it is rendered by another component, and the
overlay lands on the new element all the same.

## The hours' own modifier

`makeDragArea` gives the drags that start in the hours (an event, an edge, empty time) a modifier
of their own. Over the days, the box moves by whole days, as many as the pointer crossed, so an
event beside another keeps its place in the day; its top snaps to the quarters of an hour of the
day it started in. `containerRect` is that day where it is now: it follows the scroll, and the
snapping holds while the hours auto-scroll under a drag.

```ts [Week.vue]
const snapToWeek: Modifier = ({ transform, overlayRect, containerRect, origin }) => {
  const days = grid.value?.getBoundingClientRect();
  if (!days || !containerRect) return transform;
  const width = days.width / props.days.length;
  const column = (x: number) => Math.floor((x - days.left) / width);
  const pointer = origin.x + transform.x;
  const x = pointer < days.left || pointer >= days.right ? transform.x : (column(pointer) - column(origin.x)) * width;
  const top = overlayRect.top - containerRect.top;
  return { x, y: transform.y + Math.round(top / STEP_PX) * STEP_PX - top };
};

makeDragArea(grid, { modifiers: [snapToWeek], autoScroll: { threshold: 0.12 } });
```

The area's `autoScroll` narrows the edge that scrolls the hours, for every drag over them: the
all-day row right above stays easy to reach. Tasks and all-day events start outside the area and
move freely; the day under them shows a ghost where they would land.

## Stretching: an edge is a draggable

An edge lies inside its event's element, and a press drags the closest draggable: the edge. It has
no overlay, moves up and down only, and stays in the hours in view.

```ts [Edge.vue]
makeDraggable(el, {
  id: () => `${props.event.id}-${props.edge}`,
  type: 'edge',
  data: (): DragData => ({ kind: 'edge', event: props.event, edge: props.edge }),
  overlay: false,
  axis: 'y',
  modifiers: [restrictToFirstScrollableAncestor],
  attributes: false, // no tab stop: Shift + arrows change the end of a focused event
});
```

The edge itself doesn't move. The event grows instead, from where the edge is in the day, read
from `position` as the drop will read it:

```ts [EventBlock.vue]
const time = computed(() =>
  resizing.value && position.value
    ? resizeTo(props.event, resizing.value, position.value)
    : { start: props.event.start!, duration: props.event.duration },
);
```

## Drawing on empty time

Under the events, each day has a lane, and the lane is a draggable without an overlay. It never
moves: how far its box went (`position`) is how far the pointer went from the press, snapped to
quarters of an hour by the area. The day shows the new event as it is drawn, and its drop creates
it.

```ts [DayColumn.vue]
makeDraggable(lane, {
  id: () => `new-${props.day}`,
  type: 'new',
  data: (): DragData => ({ kind: 'new', day: props.day, from: from.value }),
  overlay: false,
  axis: 'y',
  attributes: false, // the New event button is the keyboard's way
});
```

The day's `accept` is a function: it takes any event, and only its own edges and lanes. The
all-day cells and the task list take `'event'`, a string, so the `edge` and `new` types are
refused there without a line of code. The drop is one handler:

```ts [DayColumn.vue]
onDrop: ({ active, over, position }) => {
  const data = active.data as DragData;
  if (!position) return;
  if (data.kind === 'event') {
    const place = placeOf(data.event, over, position);
    if (place) calendar.place(data.event.id, place);
  } else if (data.kind === 'edge') {
    calendar.resize(data.event.id, resizeTo(data.event, data.edge, position));
  } else {
    const { start, duration } = rangeOf(data.from, data.from + position.y);
    calendar.create(props.day, start, duration);
  }
},
```

## The keyboard

Tab to an event, pick it up with Space: the week's monitor answers the arrows,
`getKeyboardCoordinates`, with the next quarter of an hour (with Shift, an hour) or the next day.
Keyboard drags don't auto-scroll, so near an end of the hours in view the arrow scrolls them
instead. Tasks and all-day events jump from target to target (`keyboardMode: 'droppables'`) until they
are over the hours.

```ts [Week.vue]
useDnDMonitor({
  getKeyboardCoordinates: (key, { pointer, direction }) => {
    // …only over the hours
    const dy = direction.y * STEP_PX * (key.shiftKey ? 4 : 1);
    const next = { x: pointer.x + direction.x * (grid.value.offsetWidth / props.days.length), y: pointer.y + dy };
    if (canScroll && (next.y < view.top + HOUR_PX || next.y > view.bottom - HOUR_PX)) {
      hours.scrollTop += dy;
      return { x: next.x, y: pointer.y };
    }
    return next;
  },
});
```

The provider's `announcements` in `index.vue` say what was picked up and how to move it; the week
speaks the time as the arrows change it ("Tuesday, 10:30 to 11:15"), and the toast what a drop
changed. On a focused event, Delete removes it, and Ctrl+Z undoes any change.

Read more: [Your own modifier](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/constraints#your-own-modifier) ·
[Rules for a part of the page](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/constraints#rules-for-a-part-of-the-page) ·
[Leave it where it was dropped](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/drag-and-drop#leave-it-where-it-was-dropped) ·
[Without an overlay](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/drag-and-drop#without-an-overlay) ·
[Overlay components](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/overlay#overlay-components) ·

- **Page:** Dashboard
- **Source:** https://zizigy.github.io/vue-dnd-kit/docs/examples/dashboard
- **Description:** Widgets on a grid — moved by their headers, resized by their corners a cell at a time, in rows as tall as their content, with fewer columns on narrow screens.

<example height="38rem" hint="Drag a widget by its header, resize it by its corner, type in the notes" name="dashboard" title="Dashboard">



</example>

## What to look at

- **Dashboard.vue**: the grid is one sortable list with `strategy: 'grid'`, which sorts widgets
of different sizes. It counts its columns from its own width (`useElementSize`): four, three or
two. Its rows are at least 92 px tall and grow with their content, and `grid-auto-flow: dense`
fills the holes a resize leaves.
- **Widget.vue**: a widget moves by its header (`handle`), so its content stays free: the tasks
get ticked, the notes take text. Its corner is a draggable of its own, and resizes it.
- **WidgetBody.vue**: what the widgets show. Type into the notes: the row grows with the text,
and the widgets beside it with the row. Nothing measures them: it is the grid's own layout, and
the library reads the sizes as they are when a drag starts.
- **widgets.ts**: the widgets, their sizes in cells, and the grid's numbers.

Expand the demo: the grid gets four columns, and a widget made narrower on a small screen is as
wide as it was again.

## Resizing: the corner is a draggable

The corner lies inside the widget, and a press drags the closest draggable: the corner, not the
widget. It has no overlay and never moves. The widget grows instead.

```ts [Widget.vue]
makeDraggable(corner, {
  id: cornerId,
  type: 'resize',
  overlay: false,
  activation: { touch: { distance: 4 } }, // a finger resizes at once, not after a long press
  attributes: false,                       // no tab stop: Shift + arrows on the header resize
});
```

The size follows the pointer: how far it went since the press, in whole cells. The grid shows that
size while the corner is held, and its other widgets make room.

```ts [Widget.vue]
const preview = computed<Size | null>(() => {
  const start = from.value;
  if (!resizing.value || !start || !pointer.value) return null;
  return {
    w: clamp(cellsIn(pixels(own.value.w, props.cell) + pointer.value.x - start.x, props.cell), 1, props.columns),
    h: clamp(cellsIn(pixels(own.value.h, ROW) + pointer.value.y - start.y, ROW), 1, MAX_ROWS),
  };
});
```

The drop keeps it: a monitor hears the corner's `onDragEnd`. <kbd value="Escape">



</kbd>

 cancels the
drag instead, and the widget goes back to its own size.

```ts [Widget.vue]
useDnDMonitor({
  onDragEnd: ({ active: dropped }) => {
    if (dropped.id === cornerId() && preview.value) emit('resize', preview.value);
  },
});
```

## The grid sits the resize out

A corner isn't a widget, and the grid would refuse it: the drop on a target that refuses a drag is
a cancel. So while a corner is dragged, the grid is `disabled`, and the corner's drop is on no
target at all.

```ts [Dashboard.vue]
const { active } = useDnD();
const { items } = makeSortableList(grid, {
  items: widgets,
  strategy: 'grid',
  label: 'Dashboard',
  disabled: () => !!active.value?.type.includes('resize'),
});
```

## Sizes that adapt

A widget keeps the size it was given. On fewer columns it is never wider than the grid
(`Math.min(w, columns)`), and it gets its width back when the grid has room again. The rows have a
minimum height, not a height: the content decides, and the widgets in a row all stretch to the
tallest.

## The keyboard

Tab to a widget's header and press <kbd value="Space">



</kbd>

 to pick the widget up. The arrows move it
among the others, <kbd value="Space">



</kbd>

 drops it, <kbd value="Escape">



</kbd>

 puts it back. With the header
focused, <kbd value="Shift">



</kbd>

 and the arrows resize the widget a cell at a time, and screen readers
hear its new size.

- **Page:** Project board
- **Source:** https://zizigy.github.io/vue-dnd-kit/docs/examples/board
- **Description:** A product board in the spirit of Linear and Trello — columns you reorder, WIP limits, a question before Done, multi-select with a selection bar, filters the drags work through, a trash with Undo, and a card panel whose Status buttons play real drags.

<example height="40rem" hint="Drag cards and columns; click a card to open it, Ctrl/Cmd-click to select" name="board" title="Project board">



</example>

## What to look at

- **Board.vue**: the columns are a horizontal sortable list of their own (`strategy: 'horizontal'`, `axis: 'x'`), and each column is a sortable item dragged by its header
(`handle`). Expanded, the board fills the screen; on a phone it scrolls sideways.
- **Column.vue**: the cards of every column are one `group`, with the column's rules: its WIP
limit, the question before Done, and the filters. Its header meter lights up the cards a drag
would bring in.
- **Card.vue**: a sortable item of `type: 'card'`, so the trash takes cards and not columns. A
click opens it, Ctrl/Cmd-click selects it (`selected`); with the keyboard, Space picks it up,
Enter opens it and X selects it.
- **store.ts**: the board's data and rules, with no drag and drop in them, provided above the
`DnDProvider` so the overlay reads it too.

## A column's rules

Each column hands its list four rules. `put` sees every card of a multi-drag at once: the column
takes them all if they fit under its limit, or none. Over a full column the slot stays where the
drag started, the column turns red and the cards in hand say why. `onBeforeDrop` asks before
cards enter Done, and `animateChanges` slides the cards that come and go without a drag: a filter, Add
card, Undo.

```ts [Column.vue]
const { items, isOver, isAccepting } = makeSortableList(list, {
  id: props.column.id,
  items: () => props.column.cards.filter(board.matches),
  group: { name: 'cards', put: ({ keys }) => board.fits(props.column, keys) },
  overlay: CardOverlay,
  animateChanges: true,
  onBeforeDrop: (event) => (props.column.confirm && !event.sameList ? board.ask(event.items) : 'accept'),
  onDrop: (event) => {
    event.preventDefault();
    board.apply(event);
  },
});
```

## Filters, and drops the board applies

The search and the people in the toolbar filter the cards, and every drag keeps working on what
is shown. Each list reads its column through a getter, filtered, so the library never writes it:
`onDrop` calls `preventDefault()` and hands `e.result`, the new filtered cards of every column the
drop changed, to the board. The board puts them back into the places the shown cards had, and the
cards the filters hide stay where they were.

```ts [store.ts]
const merge = (all: Card[], shown: Card[]) => {
  const queue = [...shown];
  const merged: Card[] = [];
  for (const entry of all) {
    if (!matches(entry)) merged.push(entry);
    else if (queue.length) merged.push(queue.shift()!);
  }
  // Cards that came in from another column and found no place left: at the end.
  return [...merged, ...queue];
};
```

## The cards in hand

**CardOverlay.vue** is the cards' `overlay`. The grabbed card lifts and tilts, the rest of a
selection lies under it, built from `DragPreview` clones turned by their wrappers' `transform`, and
a count sits on top. Under the cards, a hint says what letting go would do, from the overlay's
`over` and `accepted`: *Move 2 cards to In review*, *Complete*, *Delete*, or *In review is full ·
2 max*. Dropped into a column, each clone lands on its own slot; over the trash the pile shrinks,
and dropped there the cards go in one after another.

```ts [CardOverlay.vue]
const hint = computed(() => {
  if (props.status !== 'dragging' || !props.over) return null;
  const many = props.items.length > 1 ? ` ${props.items.length} cards` : '';
  if (props.over.id === 'trash') return { tone: 'danger', icon: 'trash', text: `Delete${many}` };
  const column = board.column(props.over.id);
  if (!column) return null;
  if (!props.accepted) return { tone: 'danger', icon: 'limit', text: `${column.title} is full · ${column.limit} max` };
  if (board.find(props.items[0]!.id)?.column.id === column.id) return null;
  if (column.confirm) return { tone: 'done', column, text: `Complete${many}` };
  return { tone: '', column, text: `Move${many} to ${column.title}` };
});
```

A column dragged by its header is the default clone, tilted with the `rotate` property while
`data-dnd-overlay` reads `dragging`.

## Done asks first

A drop into Done returns a promise from `onBeforeDrop`: the cards wait where they were let go
while **ConfirmDialog.vue** asks. *Move to Done* answers `'accept'`, Cancel and Escape
`'reject'` (the cards fly back), and *Keep dragging* `'continue'`: the cards follow the pointer
again, and the next click drops them. Once the cards have landed (`onDragSettle`), their check
pops in Done and the sprint's progress moves.

```ts [Board.vue]
useDnDMonitor({
  onDragSettle: (event) => {
    const target = event.over ? board.column(event.over.id) : undefined;
    if ('dropped' in event && target?.confirm && event.source?.list !== target.id) board.complete(event.accepted);
  },
});
```

## Several cards, the trash and Undo

Selected cards travel together: drag one, and every selected card comes along, from any column.
The selection bar moves them, deletes them, or clears the selection (Escape does too). The
**Trash.vue** is a plain drop target that takes cards only; it deletes them from the board, as
the Delete buttons do, so the notice can put each one back where it was.

```ts [Trash.vue]
makeDroppable(el, {
  id: 'trash',
  accept: 'card',
  onDrop: (event) => {
    board.remove(event.active.ids);
    selection.delete(...event.active.ids);
  },
});
```

## Moving without a drag

A card's panel has Status buttons, and the selection bar has a button per column. They move
cards with `@vue-dnd-kit/actions`: `moveItem` plays a real keyboard drag of the card, a selected
one bringing the selection. It is announced and animated like yours, and the column's limit and
the Done question apply to it as to any drag.

```ts [store.ts]
export function useMove() {
  const board = inject(BOARD)!;
  const { moveItem } = useDnDActions();
  return (ids: Key[], target: Column) => {
    if (!board.fits(target, ids)) return board.notify(`${target.title} is full: ${target.limit} cards at most`);
    void moveItem(ids[0]!, { list: target.id });
  };
}
```

## Keyboard and screen readers

Only Space picks a card up, so Enter is free to open it; the instructions say so. The arrows move
a card by slots, and across to the next column that takes it: a full one is skipped, and past
the last column the next press carries the card on to the trash. The announcements name cards and
columns instead of ids: *"Picked up VDK-45, Haptics on Android tablets. Todo, position 6 of 6."*,
*"In review is full: its limit is 2 cards."*

```vue [index.vue]
<DnDProvider
  :keyboard="{ keys: { start: ['Space'] } }"
  screen-reader-instructions="Space picks up a card or a column, the arrow keys move it, Space drops it, Escape cancels. Enter opens a card, X selects it."
  :announcements="announcements"
  :haptics="{ enter: true, refuse: true }"
>
```

- **Page:** Block editor
- **Source:** https://zizigy.github.io/vue-dnd-kit/docs/examples/block-editor
- **Description:** A Notion-like page — blocks dragged by their handles and nested sideways, a selection box that moves several at once, new blocks dragged out of a "/" menu or a sidebar, copies with Alt, and Undo for all of it.

<example height="40rem" hint="Drag ⋮⋮ to move a block, sideways to nest it; type / for new blocks" name="block-editor" title="Block editor">



</example>

Every block has a handle (⋮⋮) and a "+" in the margin. Type in any block: Enter starts the
next one, Tab nests it, "/" opens the menu of new blocks, and Markdown works ("## ", "- ",
"<span>



</span>

 "). Draw a box in the margin to select several blocks, then drag them together. Expand the
frame: on a wide screen the blocks to add and the page's outline get sidebars of their own.

## What to look at

- **Page.vue**: the page is one sortable tree, with `placeholder: 'indicator'`: the page stays
still while you drag, and a line shows where the blocks land and at which level. The sheet
around the blocks is its `dropzone`, so a drop below the last block lands at the end.
- **BlockRow.vue**: one block. Only its handle drags (`handle`), so the text stays editable
and selectable. The handle is a button: a click selects the block and opens its menu, Space
picks the block up for the keyboard.
- **BlockText.vue** and **Editable.vue**: plain `contenteditable` text with the keys of an
editor. Typing goes from the DOM into the model; the model goes back into the DOM only when
something else changed it (Undo, a merge), so the caret never jumps.
- **editor.ts**: the document and every edit to it, with no drag and drop in it: split, merge,
indent, duplicate, turn into, and a history that takes back drops and typing alike.

## Nesting by dragging sideways

```ts [Page.vue]
const { items } = makeSortableTree(root, {
  id: 'page',
  items: editor.blocks,
  group: 'blocks',
  placeholder: 'indicator',
  nesting: 'offset',        // sideways: every 24px is a level
  indentation: INDENT,
  maxDepth: MAX_DEPTH,
  canNest: (_block, parent) => !!KINDS[parent.kind].nests,
  collapsed: editor.collapsed,
  clone: copyBlock,         // Alt-drag copies a block with what is nested in it
  createItem: (active) => createBlock((active.data as { kind: BlockKind }).kind),
  animateChanges: true,
  overOverlay: BlockGhost,
  dropzone: sheet,
  onDrop, // see Undo, below
});
```

`nesting: 'offset'` takes the level from the drag's sideways offset only: hovering the middle of
a paragraph doesn't drop into it, as in a document editor. `canNest` says which blocks take
nested blocks (paragraphs, lists, to-dos, toggles, quotes, callouts; not headings, code or
images), and when the block above refuses, the line stays at the deepest level that passes. A closed toggle
(`collapsed`) still takes blocks: a line one level in under it puts them inside, first.

Each row draws the line from its `indicator`, from the level the drop lands at. Numbered lists
count from `items`, so "2." and "a." follow every drop and every Tab. `animateChanges: true` makes the
changes no drag makes slide and fade too: Enter, Tab, Delete, Undo, a toggle opening.

```ts [BlockRow.vue]
const { indicator, selected } = makeSortableItem(el, {
  id: () => props.node.key,
  handle: '.handle',
  // A mouse press on a handle drags at once; after 4px instead, a click stays a click.
  activation: { mouse: { distance: 4 } },
  // Enter opens the block's menu; Space picks the block up.
  canDrag: (event) => !('key' in event && event.key === 'Enter'),
});

const line = computed(() => {
  const at = indicator.value;
  if (!at || at.side === 'inside') return null;
  return { side: at.side, left: `${((at.depth ?? 0) - props.node.depth) * props.indent}px` };
});
```

## Selecting several

The page is a selection area: a box drawn from its margins selects the blocks it touches.
`strategy: 'select'` makes a click on the empty margin clear the selection, and `accept` keeps
the box to blocks. A click on a handle selects its block, Shift-click a run of blocks,
Ctrl/Cmd-click one more; Escape in a text selects its block. Then:

```ts [Page.vue]
const { isSelecting, style } = makeSelectionArea(scroller, {
  strategy: 'select',
  accept: 'blocks',                     // the rows' type: their group's name
  disabled: () => menu.value !== null,  // a press closes the menu first
});
```

Drag one selected block and the others come along: the tree moves them as one run, each with
what is nested in it, in reading order. Delete removes them, Ctrl/Cmd+D duplicates them, and
the handle's menu turns them into another kind. The arrows go from handle to handle, Shift
adds to the selection.

## New blocks from a menu

"+" in the margin and "/" in a block open the same menu. A click adds the block below; each
option is also a plain draggable, which the tree's `createItem` turns into a new block where it
is dropped. The sidebar of wide screens lists the same options, and there Space picks one up
for the keyboard: an arrow toward the page takes it in.

```ts [InsertOption.vue]
makeDraggable(el, {
  id: () => `new-${props.kind}${props.option ? '-option' : ''}`,
  type: 'new-block',
  data: () => ({ kind: props.kind }),
  attributes: () => !props.option, // in the menu, an option of its listbox
});
```

While an option travels, the menu fades out so the page shows where it goes, and it closes once
the new block has landed:

```ts [Page.vue]
useDnDMonitor({
  onDragStart: ({ active }) => (lifted.value = !!popover.value?.contains(active.element)),
  onDragSettle: () => {
    if (!lifted.value) return;
    lifted.value = false;
    menu.value = null;
  },
});
```

## What the drop will do

**BlockGhost.vue** is the tree's `overOverlay`: while a drag is over the page, it wraps the
drag's own overlay (`<slot />`, the clone of the blocks or of the option) with a count and a
note. `to.parentKey` names the block the drop would go into, and `mode` says when it copies.

```vue [BlockGhost.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
const props = defineProps<{ items: DragItem[]; mode: DragMode; to: DropDestination | null }>();

// A new block: a kind dragged from the menu or the sidebar, by its `type`.
const adding = computed(() => props.items[0]?.type.includes('new-block'));

const note = computed(() => {
  const verb = props.mode === 'copy' ? 'Copy' : adding.value ? 'Add' : null;
  const parent = props.to?.parentKey == null ? undefined : editor.get(String(props.to.parentKey));
  if (!parent) return verb; // a plain move at the page's top level needs no words
  return `${verb ? `${verb} into` : 'Into'} “${parent.text}”`; // "Copy into “Open questions”"
});
</script>

<template>
  <div class="ghost">
    <slot />
    <span v-if="items.length > 1" class="count">{{ items.length }}</span>
    <span v-if="note" class="note">{{ note }}</span>
  </div>
</template>
```

## Undo

The tree writes each drop into `editor.blocks`, a writable ref. Its `onDrop` runs just before
that write, so it records the page as it was, and Undo takes the drop back. Every other edit
records itself the same way; the keystrokes typed in one block make a single step.

```ts [Page.vue]
onDrop: (event) => {
  editor.record(); // the library writes the drop after this: Undo takes it back
  const first = event.items[0]!.id;
  if (event.mode === 'insert') editor.focus(first, 'start');
  else editor.focusHandle(first);
},
```

```ts [editor.ts]
/** Called before every change: the state it changes goes on the undo stack. */
const record = () => {
  past.value = [...past.value.slice(-99), capture()];
  future.value = [];
  typing = null;
};
```

The history holds copies of the blocks with their ids, so a block keeps its row and its
selection across Undo and Redo. After a drop, a new block takes the caret, and a moved one
gives the focus to its handle: its row moved in the page, which drops the focus, and the
shortcuts go on working from the handle.

## Keyboard and screen readers

Escape in a text selects the block and focuses its handle. From there Space picks it up, the
arrows move the line (left and right: a level out or in), Space drops it; Enter opens its menu,
Delete removes it. The provider's `announcements` speak blocks by their kind and text ("Picked
up to-do list “Freeze the API”"), and the top bar's status line speaks what the buttons and
shortcuts do.

- **Page:** Chess
- **Source:** https://zizigy.github.io/vue-dnd-kit/docs/examples/chess
- **Description:** A chess board — legal moves light up, the piece in hand says why a square is refused, a pawn asks what it becomes, and a bot plays back with real drags.

<example height="36rem" hint="Drag a white piece, or Tab and Space; Bot plays Black" name="chess" title="Chess">



</example>

## What to look at

- **Square.vue**: each of the 64 squares is a drop target whose `accept` is a function. It is
asked while a piece is dragged, so the square takes that piece's legal moves only; a drop
anywhere else is refused and the piece flies back. The legal squares light up from
`isAccepting`: no state of the game's own tracks the drag.
- **Piece.vue**: a plain draggable, `disabled` when it isn't its side's turn. `keyboardMode: 'droppables'` makes the arrow keys jump between the squares that accept the piece: its legal
moves, nothing else. `snapCenterToCursor` keeps the piece centered under the pointer, and a touch
drags at once (`activation`). `canDrag` keeps your hands off the bot's pieces and off the board
while code plays, without disabling anything: drags started by code have no input event, so
`canDrag` isn't asked for them.
- **chess.ts** and **game.ts**: the rules and the game, with no drag and drop in them: legal
moves with check, castling, en passant, promotion, draws for lack of material, the notation,
undo. A move in `onDrop` makes a new position, and the overlay lands on the moved piece.

## The piece in hand

**PieceOverlay.vue** is the pieces' `overlay` component. It reads the props every overlay gets
and says what a drop on the square under it would do: over a refused square (`over` set,
`accepted` false) the piece turns red and gives the reason, over a capture it shows a target and
what it takes. Once the drop is decided (`status: 'dropping'`) the hint goes and the piece settles.

```ts [PieceOverlay.vue]
const props = defineProps<{
  active: Active;
  over: Over | null;
  accepted: boolean;
  status: DnDStatus;
}>();

const hint = computed(() => {
  const square = props.over ? String(props.over.id) : null;
  if (props.status !== 'dragging' || !square || square === piece.value.square) return null;
  if (props.accepted) {
    const taken = game.takes(piece.value.id, square);
    return taken ? { type: 'capture', text: `Takes ${NAMES[taken.kind]}` } : null;
  }
  // "Pinned", "King in check", "Not a legal move"
  return { type: 'refused', text: game.whyNot(piece.value.id, square) };
});
```

`Board.vue` draws an arrow from the square the piece came from to the square under it, from
`useDnD()`'s `active` and `over`. The provider's `haptics` vibrates a touch drag on a legal
square and when a drop is refused; the `announcements` in `index.vue` speak the same reasons:
"f7, pinned".

## Promotion: a drop that waits for an answer

Over the last rank, a pawn in hand shows the piece it becomes: the square's own `overOverlay`
(`PromotionOverlay.vue`) takes the place of the piece's. On release, the square's `onBeforeDrop`
returns a promise, and the overlay waits on the square while **PromotionPicker.vue**, a plain
element of the page next to it, asks which piece. A piece answers `'accept'`, Escape or Cancel
`'reject'` (the pawn flies back), and Keep dragging `'continue'`: the pawn follows the pointer
again, and the next click drops it and asks again.

```ts [Square.vue]
makeDroppable(el, {
  id: props.square,
  accept: ({ active }) => game.canMove(active.id, props.square),
  // Shown instead of the piece's overlay while a pawn is over the last rank.
  overOverlay: computed(() =>
    held.value?.kind === 'P' && isLastRank(props.square) ? PromotionOverlay : undefined,
  ),
  // A promise: the drop waits on the square until the picker answers.
  onBeforeDrop: ({ active }) =>
    game.promotes(active.id, props.square) ? game.askPromotion(props.square) : 'accept',
  onDrop: ({ active }) => game.move(String(active.id), props.square),
});
```

A drop target's `onBeforeDrop` gets the plain drag event and is asked only when its `accept` took
the drag; a sortable list's gets the list's `SortableDropEvent`, with the `result` of the drop.
The target's `overOverlay` is read once more after `onDrop`, for the landing: it checks the pawn as
it was picked up (`active.data`), not the game, where it is a queen by then.

## The bot, replays and castling: drags played by code

**autoplay.ts** plays moves with `@vue-dnd-kit/actions`: the bot's (`bot.ts`, a greedy one),
**Replay**'s, and the rook's step of every castling, yours included. Each is a real drag: picked
up, glided over the board a frame at a time, dropped through the square's `accept` and `onDrop`,
announced and animated as yours are. A scripted promotion brings its piece along, so the picker
doesn't open; Escape cancels a scripted drag like any other.

```ts [autoplay.ts]
const { startDrag } = useDnDActions();

const drag = startDrag(id); // from the piece's center
for (let frame = 1; frame <= FRAMES; frame++) {
  const t = easeOut(frame / FRAMES);
  const point = { x: start.x + (end.x - start.x) * t, y: start.y + (end.y - start.y) * t };
  if (!(await drag.moveTo(point))) return false; // cancelled meanwhile (Escape)
}
return drag.drop(); // true once it has landed, false if the square refused it
```

Castling is played in two moves, as by hand: the king goes two files, then its rook is dragged
over it, so the rook never jumps.

## Captures, undo and a new game

Taken pieces go to their side's **Tray.vue**: a sortable list used for its `animateChanges` alone
(`disabled`, nothing drags there). Its `enter` is a function: a new piece flies in from the square
it was taken on, and the others make room.

```ts [Tray.vue]
makeSortableList(tray, {
  items: () => props.pieces,
  getKey: (piece) => `taken-${piece.id}`,
  disabled: true,
  animateChanges: { enter: flyIn, leave: false },
});
```

Undo and New game change the position with no drag, so **glide.ts** animates them by hand
(FLIP): every piece flies from where it was, on a square or in a tray, to where it is now.
Against the bot, Undo takes back your move together with its answer.

Read more: [Deciding a drop](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/drop-decisions) ·
[The overlay](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/overlay#targets-that-change-the-overlay) ·
[Programmatic drags](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/sensors#programmatic-drags) ·
[Data changes: `animateChanges`](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/animations#data-changes-animatechanges) ·

- **Page:** Form builder
- **Source:** https://zizigy.github.io/vue-dnd-kit/docs/examples/form-builder
- **Description:** A form builder made with Nuxt UI — fields dragged from a palette, set side by side in rows, edited in a panel, then filled in a live preview with validation and exported as Vue code.

<example height="44rem" hint="Drag a field into the form, beside another one for columns" name="form-builder" title="Form builder">



</example>

Every control here is a Nuxt UI component: the fields of the form (`UInput`, `USelect`,
`URadioGroup`, `UInputRating`, `UFileUpload`…), the panels around them, the preview's `UForm`.
Vue DnD Kit moves them. Expand the demo to full screen: the palette, the form and the settings
then sit side by side.

## What to look at

- **PaletteGroup.vue**: a section of the palette is a sortable list that only gives copies:
`group: { name: 'fields', pull: 'clone', put: false }` and `sort: false`. Its items are fields
like the form's, so a copy dragged into a row is a field like the others; `clone` gives it a
key of its own. A click (or <kbd value="Enter">



</kbd>

) adds the field without a drag.
- **FormRow.vue**: a row is two things at once, as a kanban column is: an item of the form's
list of rows, dragged by its grip, and a list of up to three fields in the palette's group.
Its `put` refuses a fourth: over a full row the field in hand turns red and says why, and a
drop there is cancelled.
- **NewRowZone.vue**: drop a field on the gap between two rows, or below the last one, and it
gets a row of its own. Those places are lists too: empty lists of the same group, whose ids
say where the new row goes.
- **FieldCard.vue**: the rows are in indicator mode (`placeholder: 'indicator'`), so nothing
moves while a field is dragged: a line beside a field shows where it will go. In a narrow
builder the fields of a row stack, and the line goes above or below them.
- **Trash.vue**: while a field of the form is dragged, the palette becomes a trash: a plain
drop target that takes the form's fields only (`accept: 'fields'`, their group's name) and
removes them with `event.source.remove()`.
- **OptionList.vue**: the options of a dropdown or a multiple choice are a sortable list of
their own in the settings panel, dragged by their grips so their text stays editable.
- **form.ts**: the form, and the only code that changes it. The lists read it and never write
it, so Undo and Redo see every change, drops included.

## A row of fields is a list in a list

The rows of the form and the fields of each row are lists of two groups, `rows` and `fields`. A
drag only ever enters the lists of its own group: a field never lands among the rows, and a row
never inside another row, however they are nested.

```ts [FormRow.vue]
// The row is an item of the form's rows, dragged by its grip...
makeSortableItem(el, { item: () => props.row, handle: grip });

// ...and a list of up to three fields side by side, in the group of the palette.
const { items, isOver, isAccepting } = makeSortableList(list, {
  id: rowList(props.row.id),
  items: () => props.row.fields,
  group: { name: 'fields', put: ({ keys }) => props.row.fields.length + keys.length <= MAX_COLUMNS },
  strategy: () => (props.stacked ? 'vertical' : 'horizontal'),
  placeholder: 'indicator',
  overlay: FieldOverlay,
  clone: cloneField, // Alt-drag copies a field
  animateChanges: true,
  onDrop: form.drop,
});
```

A new row needs a place to be dropped on. Each row holds a band over the gap above it, and the
space below the last row is one more such place: an empty list of the `fields` group, which never
shows an item. Over a band the list is `isOver`, and the band draws its line. The bands take the
pointer only while something is dragged (`html[data-dnd-dragging]`), so they never get in the
way of a click:

```vue [NewRowZone.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
const NONE: readonly Field[] = [];
const { isOver, isAccepting } = makeSortableList(el, {
  id: newRowList(props.before), // 'new:<row id>', or 'new:end'
  items: () => NONE,
  group: 'fields',
  placeholder: 'indicator',
  // A band across the page: up and down are the keys that cross it, to the next list.
  strategy: 'horizontal',
  onDrop: form.drop,
});
</script>

<template>
  <div
    ref="el"
    class="pointer-events-none absolute inset-x-0 -top-[18px] z-10 h-6 in-data-[dnd-dragging]:pointer-events-auto"
  >
    <span class="… bg-primary" :class="isOver ? 'opacity-100' : 'opacity-0'" />
  </div>
</template>
```

The keyboard finds the bands as well. A keyboard drag goes from list to list by their places on
the page, with the arrows across a list: up and down for the rows, which are horizontal, and for
the bands, horizontal too. So <kbd value="ArrowUp">



</kbd>

 and <kbd value="ArrowDown">



</kbd>

 visit the rows
and the gaps between them in turn.

## One store, one Undo: lists that never write

Every list of the builder gets its items from a getter, so the library never writes them (a
[controlled list](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/shared-lists#controlled-lists)). Their `onDrop` is `form.drop`: it
cancels the write and hands `event.result`, the new arrays of every list the drop changes, to the
form. The list ids say what each array is: the fields of a row, the order of the rows, or a row
to make.

```ts [form.ts]
function apply(result: ReadonlyMap<Key, unknown[]>) {
  commit(() => {
    const created: [before: string, fields: Field[]][] = [];
    for (const [list, items] of result) {
      const [type, id] = String(list).split(':') as [string, string];
      if (list === ROWS) state.rows = items as Row[];
      else if (type === 'row') state.rows.find((row) => row.id === id)!.fields = items as Field[];
      else if (type === 'new' && items.length) created.push([id, items as Field[]]);
    }
    for (const [before, items] of created) {
      const index = state.rows.findIndex((row) => row.id === before);
      state.rows.splice(index < 0 ? state.rows.length : index, 0, row(...items));
    }
  });
}

/** `onDrop` of every list: applies the drop, and selects a field that was just added. */
function drop(event: SortableDropEvent<unknown>) {
  event.preventDefault();
  apply(event.result);
  if (event.mode === 'copy') selectedId.value = (event.items[0] as Field).id;
  forgetGone();
}
```

`commit` saves a snapshot of the form for Undo, makes the change, and removes the rows a move
left empty, all before the drop lands, so the overlay flies to where the field really is. The
trash takes the same road: `event.source.remove()` runs the row's `onDrop` with the field taken
out (`to.index` is `-1`). Typing in the settings goes through `commit` too, and keystrokes in one
setting share a key: a label typed letter by letter is a single step of Undo.

## The field in hand

The palette and the rows share one overlay component. It shows the library's copy of what is
dragged (`DragPreview`: a chip from the palette, the whole field from the form, its Nuxt UI
control included) in a frame, with a badge for what a drop would do: copy
(<kbd value="Alt">



</kbd>

), delete over the trash, nothing over a full row.

```vue [FieldOverlay.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
const props = defineProps<{ items: DragItem[]; over: Over | null; accepted: boolean; status: DnDStatus; mode: DragMode }>();

const entry = computed(() => props.items[0]!);
const state = computed(() => {
  if (props.status === 'dropping') return 'landing';
  if (props.over?.id === TRASH) return 'delete';
  // A row that refuses the field: it is full.
  if (props.over && !props.accepted) return 'full';
  // Palette fields are copies too, but they say nothing: adding is what they do.
  if (props.mode === 'copy' && !entry.value.type.includes('new-field')) return 'copy';
  return 'move';
});
</script>

<template>
  <!-- LOOKS: lifted and tilted, red when refused, smaller over the trash, flat as it lands. -->
  <div class="relative size-full rounded-md bg-default ring-2 …" :class="LOOKS[state]">
    <DragPreview :id="entry.id" class="rounded-md" :style="{ width: '100%', height: '100%' }" />
    <UBadge v-if="badge" :label="badge.label" :icon="badge.icon" :color="badge.color" size="sm" />
  </div>
</template>
```

The palette's items have a `type` of their own, `'new-field'`: the overlay tells them apart by
it, and the trash, which accepts `'fields'`, doesn't take them.

## With Nuxt UI

The docs are a Nuxt app with the `@nuxt/ui` module, and Nuxt's component auto-import reaches the
examples too: these files use `<UInput>`, `<UFormField>` or `<UTabs>` without importing them, as
a Nuxt UI project does. A Vue app with Nuxt UI's Vite plugin auto-imports them the same way;
without it, import each one: `import UButton from '@nuxt/ui/components/Button.vue'`. The types
come from `@nuxt/ui` (`import type { FormSubmitEvent } from '@nuxt/ui'`).

- **While you build, fields are pictures.** `FieldView.vue` renders a field the same way on the
canvas and in the preview: a `UFormField` around its control. On the canvas it sits in an
`inert` element, so a press on an input starts a drag instead of typing, and
<kbd value="Tab">



</kbd>

 skips the inputs. The card's toolbar (a `UFieldGroup` of buttons with
tooltips) stays out of the overlay's copy with `data-dnd-no-clone`.
- **States are Tailwind variants.** The library marks its states with attributes, which Tailwind
reads as variants: `data-[dnd-placeholder]:outline-dashed` on the field being moved,
`in-data-[dnd-overlay]:bg-default` on a row in hand, `in-data-[dnd-dragging]:pointer-events-auto`
on the bands. The colors are Nuxt UI's semantic ones (`bg-default`, `ring-primary`,
`text-error`): light and dark mode need nothing more.
- **The preview is a real UForm.** `schema.ts` makes a Zod schema from the fields, and `UForm`
validates the answers with it: `name` ties each `UFormField` to its rule, and the messages
show under the fields. Send the form to see what it submits.
- **The export** writes the same form as a component of its own: Nuxt UI controls, a Zod
schema, a `reactive` state, and the rows as grids that stack on phones.
- **The layout follows the builder's width** (`useElementSize`), not the window's: three panels
in full screen; on the page the settings take the palette's place; narrower, the palette
becomes a strip of chips above the form and the settings a sheet over it. Container queries
(`@lg:`) do the rest.

<note>

The StackBlitz button opens the files in a Vite project set up for Nuxt UI, as its docs do it for
Vue: the `@nuxt/ui/vite` plugin, Tailwind CSS, and `UApp` around the example. In a Nuxt app with
the `@nuxt/ui` module, copy the folder and render `index.vue` on a page; the form needs `zod` too.

</note>

## Keyboard and screen readers

Tab to a field and press <kbd value="Space">



</kbd>

 to pick it up. <kbd value="ArrowLeft">



</kbd>

 and
<kbd value="ArrowRight">



</kbd>

 move it along its row, <kbd value="ArrowUp">



</kbd>

 and
<kbd value="ArrowDown">



</kbd>

 to the other rows and to the gaps between them (a new row),
<kbd value="Space">



</kbd>

 drops it, <kbd value="Escape">



</kbd>

 puts it back. The provider takes only Space
for drags (`keyboard: { keys: { start: ['Space'], drop: ['Space'] } }`), which leaves
<kbd value="Enter">



</kbd>

 to open a field's settings. <kbd value="Delete">



</kbd>

 removes a field,
<kbd value="Ctrl">



</kbd>

 <kbd value="D">



</kbd>

 duplicates it, <kbd value="Ctrl">



</kbd>

 <kbd value="Z">



</kbd>

 undoes.

The provider's `announcements` speak the builder's words: "Work email: row 2, column 2 of 2",
"New date field: a new row above row 3". `form.describe` turns the position the library gives
(a list id and an index) into those words.

---

- **Page:** File manager
- **Source:** https://zizigy.github.io/vue-dnd-kit/docs/examples/file-manager
- **Description:** A cloud drive — grid and list views, a rubber band, folders that take drops everywhere and open on hover, Alt to copy, a Trash with Undo, and files dropped in from your desktop.

<example height="40rem" hint="Draw a box around files, drop them on a folder; Alt copies" name="file-manager" title="File manager">



</example>

## What to look at

- **FileView.vue**: the open folder is one sortable list, shown as a grid of tiles or a list of
rows. The rubber band, the clicks and the keys select; a drag takes the selection.
- **useFolderDrop.ts**: every folder on screen is a drop target: tiles, rows of the tree,
favorites, the crumbs of the path, the Trash. It says why it refuses a drag, and gulps when
the files are in.
- **FilesOverlay.vue**: what follows the pointer, built from the props every overlay gets: a
pile of the real tiles with a count, a "+" while Alt copies, and what the drop would do.
- **SidebarRow.vue**: a closed folder of the tree opens when a drag rests on it, so its
subfolders can take the drop. **Favorites.vue** is a sortable list of its own, whose rows
are drop targets too.
- **useDesktopDrop.ts**: files dragged in from your computer. That is the browser's drag and
drop, not the library's, handled next to it.
- **drive.ts**: the state and every change, with Undo. **index.vue**: the provider, with
the keys rebound and its announcements.

## One list, two views

The grid and the list are the same sortable list. Its options are getters, read when a drag
starts: the strategy follows the view, and a folder sorted by a column (`sort: false`) doesn't
reorder. Drags still go into its folders.

```ts [FileView.vue]
const { items } = makeSortableList(list, {
  items: drive.entries,   // the open folder, sorted by a column or in your own order
  group: 'files',
  strategy: () => (grid.value ? 'grid' : 'vertical'),
  sort: () => drive.sort.value.key === 'manual',
  multiple: 'gaps',       // the other picked files wait in place, as in Finder
  clone: drive.duplicateOf, // Alt-drag leaves the files and drops "Budget copy.xlsx"
  dropzone: area,         // the empty space takes drops too
  animateChanges: true,   // a new sort, a new folder, files sent to the Trash slide and fade
});
```

- `drive.entries` is a writable computed: the library writes each drop back through its `set`,
and the list's `onDrop` saves the drive first, for Undo.
- The window makes a new view for every folder (`:key` on `FileView`), so opening one is no
change of the list for `animateChanges` to play.

## Selecting

The provider keeps the selection; the view decides how people make it. A press on the empty
space draws a band: alone it replaces the selection, with Shift, Ctrl or Cmd held it flips the
tiles it crosses. The strategy is a getter, read when a band starts:

```ts [FileView.vue]
let adding = false;
const { isSelecting, style } = makeSelectionArea(area, {
  strategy: () => (adding ? 'toggle' : 'select'),
});

// On the area, `@pointerdown.capture`: it runs before the band's own listener.
const onPress = (event: PointerEvent) => {
  adding = event.shiftKey || event.ctrlKey || event.metaKey;
};
```

Clicks follow Finder: a click picks one, Ctrl/Cmd-click adds or removes it, Shift-click takes
the run from the last one. The arrows move a single tab stop through the files (a roving
`tabindex`, which the library leaves alone), Shift+arrows extend, Enter opens, F2 renames,
Delete sends to the Trash, typing jumps to a name. The provider gives Enter back to the app:
Space alone picks a file up.

```vue [index.vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
// Space picks a focused file up and drops it; Enter is left to open folders.
const keyboard = { keys: { start: ['Space'], drop: ['Space', 'Enter'] } };
</script>

<template>
  <DnDProvider :keyboard="keyboard" :announcements="announcements">
    <FileManager />
  </DnDProvider>
</template>
```

## Folders take drops everywhere

`useFolderDrop` makes any element a folder that takes files. A tile is also a sortable item of
the grid: there the target counts only in the middle of the tile, and near its edges the grid
makes room. `accept` refuses the folder the files are in, and a folder into itself; a refused
tile lets the grid sort over it as over any other.

```ts [useFolderDrop.ts]
const { id, isOver, isAccepting } = makeDroppable(target, {
  disabled: () => !folder(),
  data: () => drive.placeOf(folder()!),   // { name, trash, why }: the overlay reads it as `over.data`
  accept: ({ active, types }) => types.includes('files') && !drive.whyNot(active.ids, folder()!),
  onDrop: (event) => drive.dropInto(event, folder()!),
});

// The files are in once the overlay has landed in the folder: it gulps.
useDnDMonitor({
  onDragSettle: (event) => {
    if ('dropped' in event && event.dropped && event.over?.id === id.value) gulps.value++;
  },
});
```

`dropInto` moves the files, or copies them when `event.mode` is `'copy'` (Alt held over a list
with `clone`). A move calls `event.source.remove()`: the grid lets the files go, and its
`onDrop` runs with `to.index === -1`.

```ts [drive.ts]
const dropInto = (event: DnDEvent, target: FolderEntry) => {
  const dragged = entries.value.filter((entry) => event.active.ids.includes(entry.id));
  const copying = event.mode === 'copy' && !isTrash(target) && !inTrash.value;
  record(`${copying ? 'Copied' : 'Moved'} ${describe(dragged)} to ${isTrash(target) ? 'the Trash' : target.name}`);
  if (copying) return put(target, dragged.map(copyEntry), current.value);
  put(target, dragged, current.value);
  // The grid lets them go: the library writes the open folder without them.
  event.source?.remove();
  selection.delete(...event.active.ids);
};
```

A favorite is a sortable item (in `Favorites.vue`, a list of its own group) and a drop target
at once: `FavoriteRow.vue` hands the row component to `makeSortableItem`, which reads its root
element, and `SidebarRow.vue` makes the same element a folder. Near its edges a dragged
favorite sorts; files dropped on it go into its folder.

### Spring-loaded folders

A closed folder of the tree opens when a drag rests on it, as in Finder: `isOver` holds for a
moment, and the row expands. Its subfolders mount mid-drag and take drops at once.

```ts [SidebarRow.vue]
const springing = computed(() => isOver.value && props.expandable && !props.expanded);
watch(springing, (now) => {
  clearTimeout(timer);
  if (now) timer = setTimeout(() => emit('toggle'), 700);
});
```

## The overlay

`FilesOverlay.vue` is the list's `overlay`. From the grid it piles up `DragPreview`s, the real
clones of the picked tiles: dropped on a slot, each lands on its own tile; dropped into a folder,
they go in one after another. A row is as wide as the list, so the list centers the box on the
pointer (`snapCenterToCursor`) and the overlay hangs a small chip off it. The overlay is a
function, which Vue takes as a functional component: it passes on the props it reads and says
which of the two to draw.

```ts [FileView.vue]
overlay: ({ items, over, accepted, status, mode }: OverlayProps) =>
  h(FilesOverlay, { items, over, accepted, status, mode, rows: !grid.value }),
modifiers: () => (grid.value ? [] : [snapCenterToCursor]),
```

Under the pile, a pill says what letting go would do, from the folder's `data`: "Move to
Photos", "Copy to Photos" while Alt is held (`mode`), or in red why not, where `accepted` is
`false`.

```ts [FilesOverlay.vue]
const place = computed(() => (props.status === 'dragging' ? (props.over?.data as DropPlace | undefined) : undefined));
const pill = computed(() => {
  if (!place.value) return null;
  if (!props.accepted) return { refused: true, text: place.value.why ?? 'Can’t go here' };
  if (place.value.trash) return { refused: false, text: 'Move to Trash' };
  return { refused: false, text: `${props.mode === 'copy' ? 'Copy' : 'Move'} to ${place.value.name}` };
});
```

The provider's `announcements` read the same `data`, so a screen reader hears "Over Photos.
Drop to move 3 items there", or "Already in Documents". They name the files, where the
built-in texts would say their keys.

## Files from your desktop

Drag files from your computer onto the window: they upload into the folder under the pointer
(a tile, a row of the sidebar, a crumb), else into the open one, and photos show themselves.
The library drags elements of the page; files from outside come with the browser's own drag and
drop, `dragover` and `drop`, handled next to it:

```ts [useDesktopDrop.ts]
const dragover = (event: DragEvent) => {
  if (!carriesFiles(event)) return;
  // Cancelled, a `dragover` says the drop is welcome here.
  event.preventDefault();
  const folder = folderAt(event); // under the pointer: an element with a folder's `data-id`
  // …nothing goes into the Trash…
  drive.uploadTarget.value = folder.id; // that folder opens, as for the library's drags
};
```

## Undo, the Trash, and the rest

- Every change saves a copy of the drive first; the toast's Undo (or Ctrl/Cmd+Z) goes back to
it. The Trash is a folder outside the tree: what is in it remembers where it came from, and
Put Back takes it there.
- `ContextMenu.vue` (a right click, Shift+F10 or the "⋯" button) acts on the selection, or on
the open folder: Rename in place, Duplicate, Add to Favorites, Move to Trash, Empty Trash.
- The window fills the stage when you expand it, and the info pane opens beside the files. On a
phone the sidebar is a drawer; a tap opens a folder and a long press picks a file up.

[Drop into a sortable item](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/drag-and-drop#drop-into-a-sortable-item) ·
[`DragPreview`](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/overlay#dragpreview-the-clone-in-your-layout) ·
[Data changes: `animateChanges`](https://zizigy.github.io/docs/guides/animations#data-changes-animatechanges) ·
